Symptoms & causes.page_title: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) — Abnormal uterine bleeding
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Irregular or heavy bleeding can result from absent ovulation; this is more common in the first years after menstruation begins and during perimenopause, and can occur with polycystic ovary syndrome or hypothyroidism. Fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, bleeding disorders, medications, pregnancy-related conditions, pelvic inflammatory disease, and endometrial cancer are among the possible causes.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) — Abnormal uterine bleeding
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation may include history and pelvic examination, complete blood count, pregnancy and sexually transmitted-infection testing, and—depending on symptoms and age—ultrasound, hysteroscopy, sonohysterography, MRI, CT, or endometrial biopsy. Treatment may begin with hormonal contraception, progestin-only methods, tranexamic acid, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; acute severe blood loss may require fluids or transfusion.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Adenomyosis-Adenomyosis - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic
Symptoms & causes.summary: Endometrial-like tissue grows into the uterine muscle and responds to menstrual cycling, which can enlarge the uterus and cause heavy or prolonged periods, severe cramps, persistent pelvic pain, painful sex, or pelvic tenderness; some people have few symptoms. The precise cause is unknown; proposed mechanisms include tissue invasion after uterine injury, developmental tissue, postpartum inflammation, stem-cell changes, or retrograde menstruation, and growth is estrogen-dependent. Prior uterine procedures, childbirth, and middle age are associated factors. Heavy bleeding can cause anemia, and pregnancy complications or fertility effects are possible.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Endometrial tissue grows into the uterine muscle and continues its monthly thickening and bleeding there; this may enlarge the uterus and produce pain or heavy periods.
Symptoms often ease after menopause. Hormonal treatment can control bleeding and pain; hysterectomy removes the condition.
proposed mechanisms include tissue invasion after uterine injury, developmental tissue, postpartum inflammation, stem-cell changes, or retrograde menstruation, and growth is estrogen-dependent

heading_notes.heading: Adenomyosis
notes: The defining change is misplaced uterine-lining tissue within the muscular uterine wall, where it responds to menstrual cycling.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Some people have no symptoms or only mild discomfort.

Possible effects include prolonged or heavy menstruation, severe period cramps or sharp pelvic pain, persistent pelvic pain, pain with sex, and uterine enlargement with lower abdominal tenderness or pressure.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause remains uncertain. Proposed explanations include uterine-lining cells entering muscle after surgery, developmental tissue placement, postpartum inflammation, stem-cell changes, and menstrual flow moving backward into the pelvis.
Estrogen supports the condition’s growth regardless of how it begins.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior uterine procedures, childbirth, and middle age are associated with adenomyosis; cases also occur in younger adults.
Fibroids and endometriosis may coexist, and overlapping symptoms can complicate diagnosis.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Heavy bleeding can cause anemia, with fatigue, breathlessness, and related effects.
Pain and unpredictable bleeding may restrict daily activities and create concern about leakage.
Pregnancy associations include miscarriage, preterm delivery, and small-for-gestational-age birth; a possible infertility link needs further study.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Adenomyosis-Adenomyosis - Diagnosis & treatment - Mayo Clinic
headings: What to expect from your doctor
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation distinguishes adenomyosis from fibroids, endometriosis, and endometrial polyps. A pelvic exam, transvaginal ultrasound, and MRI may help; biopsy may rule out other disease but does not confirm adenomyosis, which is definitively identified only by examining the uterus after hysterectomy. Treatment is symptom- and life-stage-based: NSAIDs for pain and bleeding, combined hormonal contraception or progestin methods (including an IUD) to reduce bleeding, and hysterectomy when symptoms are severe and other options fail. Warm baths and a heating pad may ease cramps.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Symptoms overlap with fibroids, endometriosis, and uterine polyps, so clinicians may first investigate these alternatives.
Pelvic examination may find an enlarged or tender uterus; transvaginal ultrasound and MRI can show uterine features.
Endometrial sampling may rule out other serious disease but does not establish adenomyosis. Definitive confirmation requires examination of the uterus after hysterectomy.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: This resource area links to descriptions of MRI, pelvic examination, and ultrasound.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on symptom burden and proximity to menopause, when symptoms often subside.
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen may reduce pain and bleeding when started shortly before menstruation.
Combined hormonal contraception and progestin methods, including an IUD or continuous pills, can reduce bleeding and pain; some methods stop periods.
Hysterectomy may be considered for severe symptoms after other approaches fail; ovary removal is not required to treat adenomyosis.

heading_notes.heading: Self care
notes: Warm bathing, a lower-abdominal heating pad, and an anti-inflammatory medicine may ease cramping and pelvic pain.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: A primary-care clinician or gynecologist may evaluate the problem; prepare to discuss menstrual and reproductive history, symptoms, medicines, and questions.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track when symptoms began and how they relate to periods; bring a complete list of medicines and supplements and relevant menstrual, pregnancy, and birth history.
Useful questions cover likely causes, testing, symptom medicines, surgery, and possible effects on pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: The clinician may ask about symptom timing and severity, last period, pregnancy possibility, contraception, menstrual links, and factors that improve or worsen symptoms.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Adnexal tumors and masses - Symptoms and causes
headings: Living with adnexal tumors and masses?
Symptoms & causes.summary: These are growths in or around the ovaries, fallopian tubes, and nearby connective tissue; many are benign, though some are cancerous, and many cause no symptoms. Possible symptoms include pelvic or abdominal pain or pressure, painful periods or sex, early fullness, nausea, bloating, bowel or urinary changes, unusual vaginal bleeding, or fever. Causes include cysts, endometriosis, ectopic pregnancy, fibrosis, blocked tubes, infection/abscess, and ovarian torsion. Cancer risk is higher after menopause and with relevant family history or inherited variants; hormone fertility medicines and smoking are also noted risk factors.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Adnexal masses are growths involving the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or their supporting tissue; many are benign, but some are cancerous.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Amenorrhea - Symptoms and causes
Symptoms & causes.summary: Amenorrhea means absent menstrual periods. Primary amenorrhea is no first period by age 15 when other puberty changes are present, or by 13 without them; secondary amenorrhea includes missing at least three periods after prior menstruation, or a prolonged absence with irregular cycles. Pregnancy is a common cause of secondary amenorrhea. Other causes include expected states (pregnancy, breastfeeding, menopause), hormonal contraception, certain medicines, stress, low energy intake, intense exercise, PCOS, thyroid or pituitary disorders, ovarian insufficiency, and reproductive-tract structural conditions. Associated signs can include milky nipple discharge, hot flashes, vaginal dryness, hair loss, headaches, vision changes, facial hair, pelvic pain, or acne. Risks include family history, eating disorders, severe anxiety, athletic training, and uterine procedures; underlying causes may affect fertility and bone health.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia (U.S. National Library of Medicine) — Amniotic band syndrome
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: The condition is a group of rare birth defects in which strands from the amniotic sac wrap around fetal body parts; affected areas can include the abdomen, chest, face, limbs, fingers, or toes. Amnion damage can produce bands that trap or compress developing parts, reduce their blood supply, and cause abnormal development or amputation; severity ranges from a small indentation to a missing or severely underdeveloped body part.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis may be made by prenatal ultrasound when the abnormality is sufficiently severe or by physical examination of the newborn. Symptoms & causes.page_title: Anterior vaginal prolapse (cystocele) - Symptoms and causes
Symptoms & causes.summary: A weakened pelvic floor allows the bladder to bulge into the front wall of the vagina. Mild prolapse may cause no symptoms; otherwise there may be pelvic or vaginal pressure, a visible or felt bulge, worsening pressure with coughing, lifting, or straining, and urinary hesitancy, incomplete emptying, frequency, or leakage. Symptoms may worsen after standing and improve when lying down. Pregnancy and vaginal birth, aging and lower estrogen after menopause, hysterectomy, obesity, inherited connective-tissue weakness, heavy lifting, constipation/straining, and chronic cough can contribute. Difficulty emptying the bladder can raise the chance of bladder infections.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Anterior vaginal prolapse (cystocele) - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
headings: What to expect from your doctor
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis uses medical and pregnancy history plus a pelvic exam, often while bearing down and contracting pelvic-floor muscles; bladder-emptying and urine tests may be added. Options depend on symptoms and can include observation, pelvic-floor muscle exercises/therapy, or a vaginal pessary for support. Surgery may reposition and support the bladder if other approaches do not help. If uterine prolapse is also present, repair may be combined with hysterectomy or a uterus-preserving procedure. Surgery may be deferred when future pregnancy is planned; prolapse can recur.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Dreisler and Kjer, Asherman’s syndrome: current perspectives on diagnosis and management (PMC/International Journal of Women’s Health) — Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions)
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Asherman syndrome consists of intrauterine or endocervical adhesions and can be associated with reduced menstrual flow or absent periods, pain, reduced fertility, pregnancy loss, and abnormal placentation. The main cause is injury to the endometrial basal layer, most often after curettage of a recently pregnant uterus; it can also follow hysteroscopic surgery, uterine artery embolization, or genital tuberculosis.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Contrast sonohysterography or hysterosalpingography can assist initial evaluation, while hysteroscopy is the definitive diagnostic method; MRI may be useful when the uterine cavity is completely obliterated. Symptomatic disease with infertility or painful hypo- or amenorrhea is treated by hysteroscopic division of adhesions, using scissors or other hysteroscopic instruments.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Fetal–maternal incompatibility in the Rh system. Rh isoimmunization associated with hereditary spherocytosis: case presentation and review of the literature (PMC) — Atypical isoimmunization
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Maternal sensitization occurs when fetal red blood-cell antigens enter the maternal circulation; IgG antibodies formed after subsequent exposure can cross the placenta. Fetal hemolysis may cause anemia, hypoxia, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, generalized edema, hydramnios, or fetal loss. More than 50 red-cell alloantibodies besides anti-D have been associated with hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Maternal antibody titers can be measured with an indirect Coombs test; ultrasound and Doppler assessment of fetal blood flow help monitor fetal status. When fetal anemia is suspected, amniotic-fluid assessment and cordocentesis can evaluate disease severity; cordocentesis can also provide a route for fetal transfusion. Severe early disease may be managed with plasmapheresis, while selected cases require intrauterine transfusion or delivery when fetal maturity permits.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Bacterial vaginosis - Symptoms and causes
Symptoms & causes.summary: BV is an imbalance in vaginal bacteria, with overgrowth of anaerobes relative to protective lactobacilli. It may cause thin gray, white, or green discharge, a fishy odor, itching, or burning with urination, but many people have no symptoms. It is more common during reproductive years; douching and having a new or multiple sex partners are associated factors, though the relationship with sex is not fully clear. BV may raise the risk of sexually transmitted infections and infection after gynecologic surgery; possible links with pelvic inflammatory disease and pregnancy complications are also described.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: A clinician evaluates symptoms and may use a pelvic exam and vaginal-fluid testing to identify the bacterial imbalance and distinguish other causes. Treatment may include prescribed metronidazole, clindamycin, tinidazole, or secnidazole; the form and precautions differ. Complete the prescribed course because recurrence can occur. Partner testing or treatment may be relevant for a symptomatic female partner. Avoid douching; use unscented products and safer-sex practices to reduce irritation and infection risk.

diagnosis: A clinician evaluates symptoms and vaginal fluid to identify BV and distinguish it from yeast, trichomoniasis, or other conditions.

A clinician evaluates symptoms and may use a pelvic exam and vaginal-fluid testing to identify the bacterial imbalance and distinguish other causes. Treatment may include prescribed metronidazole, clindamycin, tinidazole, or secnidazole; the form and precautions differ. Complete the prescribed course because recurrence can occur. Partner testing or treatment may be relevant for a symptomatic female partner. Avoid douching; use unscented products and safer-sex practices to reduce irritation and infection risk.
Examination checks vaginal discharge and may collect a sample for testing.
treatment_and_self_care: Prescription options include metronidazole, clindamycin, tinidazole, or secnidazole in oral or vaginal forms; follow instructions and precautions.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Fetal Lower Urinary Tract Obstruction (LUTO): a practical review for providers (NCBI/PMC) — Bladder outlet obstruction
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Prenatal findings typically include a markedly enlarged, sometimes thick-walled bladder and bilateral upper urinary-tract dilation; a keyhole sign may occur. Posterior urethral valves and urethral atresia are the two most common causes, with posterior urethral valves generally affecting male fetuses and urethral atresia more often identified in female fetuses. Severe obstruction can produce oligohydramnios, renal dysplasia, and secondary pulmonary hypoplasia.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation includes detailed anatomic ultrasound, echocardiography, fetal sex and amniotic-fluid assessment, genetic evaluation, and serial imaging. When intervention is considered, ultrasound-guided bladder drainage and fetal-urine testing can help assess renal function and genetic status. Potential fetal treatments include vesicoamniotic shunting, fetal cystoscopy with treatment of posterior urethral valves, or vesicostomy; evidence for benefit remains limited.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Bleeding during pregnancy
headings: Typical vaginal bleeding near the end of pregnancy
From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Symptoms & causes.summary: Vaginal bleeding during pregnancy can occur for many reasons. First-trimester bleeding is relatively common and does not always mean a pregnancy is in trouble, but it can also signal miscarriage or another condition needing prompt care. Report any bleeding to a pregnancy-care professional and describe the amount, appearance, and whether clots or tissue passed. The linked Mayo Clinic page covers causes and when to seek care; it does not provide a paired diagnosis-and-treatment page.

heading_notes.heading: Definition
notes: Vaginal bleeding during pregnancy ranges from light spotting to heavy bleeding; significance depends on gestational stage and associated symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Causes vary by trimester and include implantation/cervical changes, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental problems, labor, and other pregnancy complications.
The linked Mayo Clinic page covers causes and when to seek care

heading_notes.heading: First trimester
notes: Early bleeding can occur in healthy pregnancies but may also indicate miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy; report it to the pregnancy-care team.

heading_notes.heading: Second or third trimester
notes: Later bleeding can be associated with placenta previa, placental abruption, preterm labor, or cervical changes and needs prompt evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: Typical vaginal bleeding near the end of pregnancy
notes: A small amount of blood-tinged mucus can occur as the cervix changes near labor; heavier bleeding is not typical.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Contact a clinician for any pregnancy bleeding; emergency evaluation is needed for heavy bleeding, severe pain, fainting, or other serious symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Second trimester
notes: Causes include pregnancy loss, cervical or placental problems, and preterm labor.

heading_notes.heading: Third trimester
notes: Potential causes include placenta previa/abruption and labor-related cervical change.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation depends on gestational age, amount and duration of bleeding, and associated symptoms. Mayo Clinic advises reporting pregnancy bleeding to a healthcare professional; moderate or heavy bleeding, tissue passage, pain, cramping, fever, chills, or later-pregnancy bleeding require prompt contact. Possible causes range from implantation bleeding to miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental disorders, cervical or vaginal conditions, and labor. The source does not prescribe one treatment for bleeding as a symptom.

Symptoms & causes.summary: Cancer is a broad group of diseases in which abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and may invade nearby tissue or spread. Symptoms depend on the cancer location; possible general warning signs include persistent fatigue, a new lump, unexplained weight change, skin changes or a sore that does not heal, bowel or bladder changes, persistent cough, swallowing difficulty, hoarseness, indigestion, unexplained pain or fever, night sweats, or unusual bleeding/bruising. Cancer develops through DNA changes; these can arise for varied reasons, and many cases occur without a known risk factor. Prevention measures include avoiding tobacco, limiting UV exposure, healthy eating, regular activity, and recommended screening.

heading_notes.heading: What do gene mutations do?
notes: Mutations can switch growth signals on, disable growth brakes, or prevent abnormal cells from dying.

heading_notes.heading: What causes gene mutations?
notes: Changes may be inherited, arise during cell division, or result from carcinogens such as tobacco, radiation, or chemicals.

notes: Multiple genetic changes can accumulate and interact before a cell becomes malignant.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Cervical Cancer Treatment During Pregnancy (PDQ), National Cancer Institute — Cancer during pregnancy
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Selected early-stage cervical cancers may be managed with fertility-sparing conization or radical trachelectomy, depending on disease features and timing. For some less-aggressive early cancers without lymphatic spread, treatment may be postponed until fetal viability or after pregnancy; positive nodes generally favor immediate treatment. For stage II or greater cervical disease, delaying treatment is generally inappropriate; curative-intent chemotherapy and radiation are standard, with radiation toxic to the fetus. Most chemotherapy agents can be administered from the second trimester onward in selected circumstances, but fetal growth restriction is a reported risk.

Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, has been ranked among the best Obstetrics and Gynecology hospitals in the nation by U.S. News & World Report.
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Screening uses Pap testing and HPV testing to find abnormal or precancerous cells; colposcopy and biopsy can assess abnormal results, and imaging or other tests establish stage. Treatment depends on stage, health, and fertility goals. Small cancers may be treated with cone biopsy or trachelectomy to preserve the uterus; hysterectomy is used for some localized cancers. Radiation, often combined with chemotherapy, is used for disease beyond the cervix or after surgery when recurrence risk is elevated. Targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and palliative care may be used in advanced disease.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Cholestasis of pregnancy - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Symptoms & causes.summary: This pregnancy-related liver condition usually occurs later in pregnancy and reduces bile flow, allowing bile acids to build up. The main symptom is intense itching without a rash, often on palms and soles and worse at night; jaundice, nausea, appetite loss, or oily foul-smelling stools can also occur. Pregnancy hormones, genetic factors, and environment may contribute. Prior cholestasis, liver or gallbladder disease, multiple pregnancy, and older maternal age are associated risks, and recurrence in later pregnancies is common. Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Assessment includes symptoms and history, physical examination, and blood tests for bile acids and liver function. Treatment aims to relieve itching and reduce fetal risk: a clinician may prescribe ursodiol or another medicine, and may arrange fetal monitoring with nonstress testing or a biophysical profile. After a prior episode, contraception without estrogen may be preferred because estrogen-containing methods can trigger recurrence.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Chronic pelvic pain - Symptoms and causes
Symptoms & causes.summary: Chronic pelvic pain is pain below the bellybutton and between the hips lasting six months or longer. It may be steady or intermittent, aching, sharp, cramping, heavy, or pressure-like; it can worsen with sex, urination, bowel movements, or prolonged sitting/standing and may disrupt sleep, work, or exercise. Urinary urgency/frequency, bloating, nausea, constipation, or diarrhea can accompany it. Causes may be multiple and include endometriosis, pelvic-floor or musculoskeletal conditions, nerve injury, bladder or bowel disorders, and other pelvic disease; sometimes tests find no single cause.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Chronic pelvic pain - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
headings: What to expect from your doctor
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation combines symptom and family history, a pain diary, pelvic exam, lab testing, ultrasound or other imaging, and sometimes laparoscopy to identify causes such as endometriosis or infection. Treatment targets an identified cause when possible; otherwise it focuses on symptom control and quality of life. Options can include pain relievers, hormonal medicines for cycle-related pain, antibiotics for bacterial causes, selected medicines for chronic pain, pelvic-floor physical therapy, biofeedback or other supportive therapies, and pain-rehabilitation programs. Surgery is reserved for a treatable cause; hysterectomy or ovary removal is uncommon and has major consequences.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia — Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM)
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: CCAM is a benign prenatal lung lesion composed of abnormal, nonfunctioning lung tissue that usually grows in one lung lobe. Its cause is unknown; it is not linked to a known gene or chromosomal abnormality and is not hereditary. Large lesions can restrict lung growth, shift the heart, and lead to fetal hydrops; small lesions often cause no prenatal or postnatal breathing problems.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
notes: CCAM is a benign prenatal lung lesion composed of abnormal, nonfunctioning lung tissue that usually grows in one lung lobe.
Its cause is unknown; it is not linked to a known gene or chromosomal abnormality and is not hereditary.
Large lesions can restrict lung growth, shift the heart, and lead to fetal hydrops; small lesions often cause no prenatal or postnatal breathing problems.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia — Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation (CCAM)
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Routine prenatal ultrasound commonly detects CCAM as a bright area representing a cyst or mass in the fetal lung. High-resolution fetal ultrasound and serial monitoring, including calculation of the CCAM volume ratio, help assess lesion growth and guide management. Small lesions may be monitored during pregnancy and removed after birth; selected large or high-risk lesions may require treatment before birth, and postnatal surgery may be needed.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) - CON-20472981-Symptoms and causes
Symptoms & causes.summary: CDH is a birth condition in which the diaphragm does not close fully, leaving an opening through which abdominal organs can move into the chest. This can restrict lung development and affect both lungs, pulmonary blood pressure, the heart, and abdominal organs; severity ranges from mild to life-threatening. The cause is often unknown, though genetic changes or syndromes can be involved. Complications can include breathing and digestive problems, infections, hearing loss, reflux, growth or developmental difficulties, and chest/spine changes.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: CDH is usually detected on fetal ultrasound; repeated ultrasound, fetal MRI, fetal echocardiography, and genetic testing may assess severity and associated conditions. Care is coordinated by an experienced maternal-fetal and neonatal team. Pregnancy monitoring is frequent; fetoscopic tracheal balloon treatment is being studied for selected severe cases. Delivery may be vaginal or by C-section according to clinical circumstances. After birth, care may involve NICU support, ventilation, and ECMO for severe heart-lung problems; the diaphragm opening is generally repaired when the baby's condition allows.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia — Congenital high airway obstruction syndrome (CHAOS)
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: CHAOS is a rare congenital airway blockage that traps fluid in the fetal lungs, causing lung overinflation and possible compression of the heart. The underlying cause is unknown; airway obstruction may result from laryngeal atresia, tracheal stenosis, or a web-like membrane. Prenatal ultrasound may show bilaterally enlarged, bright fetal lungs with dilated airways and a downward-displaced diaphragm; severe cases can cause hydrops.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia — Congenital high airway obstruction syndrome (CHAOS)
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation uses high-resolution fetal ultrasound and ultrafast fetal MRI to define fetal anatomy and provide additional detail about the upper airway. Because CHAOS can be associated with genetic or chromosomal conditions, fetal genetic testing such as amniocentesis may be considered. A multidisciplinary team uses the obstruction's type and location to guide treatment and delivery planning; untreated CHAOS can be life-threatening.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Conjoined twins - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Conjoined twins result when an early embryo does not fully separate; the babies remain connected, commonly at the chest, abdomen, or pelvis, and may share organs.
Outcomes vary with the joining site, shared anatomy, and specialist team; some infants are stillborn or die soon after birth, while some survivors can undergo separation.

heading_notes.heading: Conjoined twins
notes: Patterns include chest, abdominal, spinal, pelvic, trunk, and head connections; the shared structures differ by pattern and may involve heart, liver, intestines, urinary or reproductive organs, limbs, skull, or brain.
An asymmetric pair may have one much less developed twin; a very rare form has one twin partly developed within the other.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: There is no pregnancy symptom specific to conjoined twins; ordinary twin-pregnancy signs may include faster uterine growth, tiredness, nausea, and vomiting.
Ultrasound can identify the condition during pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: How twins are joined
notes: The page describes eight anatomic patterns: thoracopagus (chest), omphalopagus (near navel), pygopagus (base of spine/buttocks), rachipagus (spine), ischiopagus (pelvis), parapagus (side-by-side trunk), craniopagus (skull), and cephalopagus (head/upper body).
Shared organs and limb counts vary; chest and abdominal pairs may share liver or digestive organs, while shared heart, brain, or other vital structures affects survival and separation options.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: One theory is late incomplete splitting of a single fertilized egg, typically after the period when embryonic layers begin forming organs; another proposes early fusion of separate embryos.
The reason either process occurs is unknown.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: No established factors identify couples at increased risk because the condition is rare and its cause remains unclear.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Pregnancy usually requires planned cesarean delivery and carries elevated risks of prematurity, stillbirth, and early death.
Newborn complications can include respiratory or cardiac problems; later effects may include spinal curvature, cerebral palsy, or learning difficulties.
Risks depend on shared anatomy and the expertise of the care team; families should discuss anticipated complications and preparation with specialists.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Conjoined twins - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Routine ultrasound may identify conjoined twins as early as weeks 7–12; detailed ultrasound and fetal echocardiography around mid-pregnancy clarify connection and organ function.
Fetal MRI can add anatomic detail for care planning; after birth, testing maps each twin’s structure, function, and shared organs.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Links to echocardiography, MRI, and ultrasound explanations.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care is individualized to shared anatomy, health, and likely outcomes; specialists monitor pregnancy and coordinate delivery, often by planned C-section several weeks before the due date.
Separation is commonly considered after birth, often around 6–12 months, when the infants’ condition and anatomy permit. Emergency separation is reserved for a life-threatening problem.

Planning weighs vital-organ sharing, surgical feasibility, expected function and quality of life, and the possibility of remaining joined; if separation is not feasible, ongoing medical and comfort-focused care may be discussed.

heading_notes.heading: Monitoring during pregnancy
notes: High-risk pregnancy care tracks fetal growth, maternal health, shared anatomy, and delivery planning with specialist imaging and consultations.

heading_notes.heading: Delivery
notes: Cesarean delivery is commonly planned before term at a center with neonatal and surgical expertise.

heading_notes.heading: Separation surgery
notes: Separation is often planned after the infants have grown and been evaluated, commonly in the first year; timing depends on shared organs and stability.

heading_notes.heading: If surgery isn't an option
notes: If separation would be unsafe or is not feasible, the team may support the twins living joined with ongoing medical care and comfort-focused planning.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Families may benefit from counseling, social work, peer support, and clear discussions about options and uncertainty.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Families can expect coordinated consultations with obstetric, neonatal, surgical, and other specialists; bringing questions and support people can help with complex decisions.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about the connection site, shared organs, anticipated delivery and neonatal care, separation timing and risks, long-term function, and support resources.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Care teams discuss maternal/fetal status, imaging findings, each twin’s organ function, available treatment pathways, and family goals.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Merck Manual Professional Edition — Diaphragmatic hernia
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Diaphragmatic hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents into the chest through a defect in the diaphragm; associated pulmonary hypoplasia can cause pulmonary hypertension. Respiratory distress commonly occurs during the first hours after birth and may be immediate in severe cases; a scaphoid abdomen and reduced breath sounds over the affected side may occur.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Merck Manual Professional Edition — Diaphragmatic hernia
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis may be made by prenatal ultrasound or fetal MRI and, after birth, by chest radiograph; CT or MRI and echocardiography can further evaluate anatomy and associated disease. A neonate with respiratory distress should receive immediate endotracheal intubation and ventilation; bag-mask ventilation should be avoided, and gastric decompression is used. Surgery returns abdominal organs to the abdomen and closes the diaphragmatic defect; selected severe fetal cases may undergo fetoscopic endoluminal tracheal occlusion.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Double uterus - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: A congenital difference occurs when the paired fetal uterine structures do not fully join, leaving two uterine cavities; one or two cervices may be present, and a vaginal tissue partition can also occur.
Many people have successful pregnancies, though miscarriage and premature birth are more likely.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Often there are no symptoms and the finding emerges on pelvic examination or imaging during miscarriage evaluation.
With a divided vagina, menstrual blood may pass despite a tampon placed in only one channel; severe period pain or recurrent pregnancy loss can also prompt assessment.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for menstrual bleeding that continues despite tampon use, severe menstrual pain, or repeated miscarriage.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The exact developmental cause is unknown; family clustering suggests inherited factors may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk factors are not established; genetic and other unknown influences may be involved.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Possible associated outcomes include infertility, miscarriage, premature birth, and kidney abnormalities; many people nonetheless have routine pregnancies and deliveries.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Pelvic examination may reveal two cervices or an unusual uterine shape; imaging confirms the anatomy.

Options include abdominal or transvaginal ultrasound, sometimes 3D ultrasound; saline sonohysterography to outline the cavity; MRI; and hysterosalpingography to show uterine shape and tubal openness. Kidney imaging may be added.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Links to MRI and ultrasound.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: No intervention is usually needed without symptoms or related problems; surgery to unite uterine cavities is uncommon.

In selected cases with an unexplained pregnancy loss and a partially divided uterus, surgery may be considered to improve a future pregnancy. Removing a vaginal partition can address a divided vagina and may ease childbirth.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Evaluation may start with primary care and involve gynecology or reproductive endocrinology; check whether testing requires preparation and bring symptom, family, reproductive, and medication histories.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Prepare a symptom timeline, personal and family history, medication/supplement list, and questions about diagnosis, treatment alternatives, restrictions, and specialist referral; a companion can help retain details.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Ectopic pregnancy: Rare but potentially life-threatening-Ectopic pregnancy - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, most often in a fallopian tube, but sometimes in an ovary, abdomen, or cervix.
It cannot develop normally; untreated growth may rupture tissue and cause life-threatening internal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Ectopic pregnancy
notes: This condition-title or navigation heading identifies Ectopic pregnancy; clinical guidance is documented under the topic headings.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Early symptoms may resemble an ordinary pregnancy, including missed period, breast tenderness, and nausea; a pregnancy test can still be positive.

Early warning signs often include light vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain. Internal bleeding may cause shoulder pain or bowel pressure; rupture can cause severe internal bleeding, dizziness, fainting, or shock.

heading_notes.heading: Early warning of ectopic pregnancy
notes: Light bleeding and pelvic pain are common early clues; blood irritating nearby nerves may produce shoulder discomfort or an urge to have a bowel movement.

heading_notes.heading: Emergency symptoms
notes: Severe abdominal or pelvic pain with vaginal bleeding, marked lightheadedness/fainting, or shoulder pain require emergency care because rupture and hemorrhage are possible.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Get emergency help for the red-flag combination of severe pain and bleeding, faintness, or shoulder pain.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Tubal implantation can occur when an egg is delayed by a damaged, inflamed, or misshapen tube; hormonal imbalance or abnormal embryo development may also contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk is higher after a prior ectopic pregnancy, pelvic infection/STIs, infertility or fertility treatment, tubal surgery, smoking, and pregnancy despite an IUD or after tubal ligation.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Tubal rupture can produce severe, potentially fatal internal bleeding without prompt treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: No method guarantees prevention. Condoms and limiting STI exposure may reduce pelvic infection risk; avoiding or stopping smoking lowers a modifiable risk.

What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: A pelvic exam may identify tenderness or a mass but cannot confirm an ectopic pregnancy; blood testing and ultrasound are required.

heading_notes.heading: Pregnancy test
notes: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) testing confirms pregnancy; repeat measurements help assess whether the pregnancy is progressing normally.

heading_notes.heading: Ultrasound
notes: Transvaginal ultrasound helps locate the pregnancy and assess for an adnexal mass or internal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Transvaginal ultrasound
notes: A vaginal probe can locate a pregnancy, assess the uterus and tubes, and identify internal bleeding or an adnexal mass.

heading_notes.heading: Other blood tests
notes: Serial hCG and blood counts/type testing help assess pregnancy progression, bleeding, and treatment needs.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment depends on pregnancy location/size, hCG, symptoms, and stability; options include methotrexate, laparoscopy, or open surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Medication
notes: Methotrexate may stop growth when the patient is stable and the pregnancy is small/unruptured; hCG follow-up continues until resolved.

heading_notes.heading: Laparoscopic procedures
notes: Laparoscopy removes ectopic tissue through small abdominal incisions; the tube may be opened or removed depending on damage and fertility factors.

heading_notes.heading: Emergency surgery
notes: Rupture or severe internal bleeding requires urgent surgery; the affected tube may need removal.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: An ectopic pregnancy and its treatment can involve grief and fertility concerns; follow-up and emotional support are important.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring pregnancy dates, symptoms, medicines, and prior ectopic/tubal history; urgent symptoms require emergency care.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Follow blood-test monitoring until hCG resolves, report worsening symptoms, and ask about future pregnancy timing and risk.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Questions may cover last menstrual period, pregnancy symptoms, pain/bleeding, prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery, and fertility treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Work-up may use pelvic exam, transvaginal ultrasound, hysteroscopy, biopsy, and D&C; staging may include imaging and blood tests, with final stage sometimes determined after surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosing endometrial cancer
notes: The section organizes exam, imaging, visualization, and tissue-sampling methods used to confirm disease and plan treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic exam
notes: A clinician inspects the vulva and vagina, uses a speculum, and palpates uterus/ovaries.

heading_notes.heading: Transvaginal ultrasound
notes: A vaginal transducer images pelvic organs and assesses endometrial thickness/texture; MRI or CT may supplement it.

heading_notes.heading: Hysteroscopy
notes: A lighted scope passed through cervix directly views the uterine cavity and lining.

heading_notes.heading: Staging endometrial cancer
notes: Stage 1 is limited to the uterus; stage 4 involves nearby organs or distant spread; staging guides care.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Surgery is usually first; radiation and medicines may be added based on stage, tumor features, health, and preferences.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Hysterectomy with removal of tubes/ovaries is common; this ends pregnancy potential and causes menopause if ovaries are removed before natural menopause.
Surgeons inspect nearby structures and may sample lymph nodes for staging.

heading_notes.heading: Radiation therapy
notes: External-beam or internal brachytherapy may shrink tumors, treat disease after surgery, or serve as an option when surgery is unsafe.

heading_notes.heading: Chemotherapy
notes: Chemotherapy may be given before or after surgery or for advanced/recurrent disease.

heading_notes.heading: Hormone therapy
notes: Hormone-lowering medicines may help advanced tumors that depend on hormones.

heading_notes.heading: Targeted therapy
notes: Targeted medicines may be combined with chemotherapy for advanced disease.

heading_notes.heading: Immunotherapy
notes: Immune-based treatment may be considered when advanced cancer has not responded to other therapies.

heading_notes.heading: Palliative care
notes: Supportive care relieves symptoms and supports quality of life alongside cancer treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Learning stage/options, maintaining supportive relationships, peer groups, and usual activities can help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Prepare symptom and medicine lists and questions about stage, treatment, and side effects.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Record symptoms and medications; ask about stage, fertility effects, treatment choices, likely side effects, and support.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about abnormal bleeding, cycle/menopause history, risk factors, prior hormone therapy, and test results.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Endometriosis - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Endometriosis is endometrial-like tissue growing outside the uterus, which can inflame pelvic tissue, cause pain, and affect fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Endometriosis
notes: This condition-title or navigation heading identifies Endometriosis; clinical guidance is documented under the topic headings.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Cyclic pelvic pain, severe cramps, painful sex, bowel or urination pain, heavy bleeding, infertility, fatigue, bloating, nausea, constipation/diarrhea may occur; some people have no symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care for persistent or severe pelvic pain that disrupts daily life.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause is uncertain; theories include retrograde menstruation, cellular transformation, embryonic remnants, surgical implantation, immune factors, and cell transport.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Early menstruation, short cycles, long/heavy periods, low body mass, blocked outflow, and family history may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Adhesions and ovarian endometriomas may form; infertility is a key concern, and chronic pain or rare cancer associations may occur.

heading_notes.heading: Infertility
notes: Endometriosis can affect fertility through inflammation, scarring, and impaired ovarian/tubal function.

heading_notes.heading: Fertilization and implantation
notes: Endometriosis can alter pelvic anatomy or inflammation around ovaries and tubes, potentially interfering with egg pickup, fertilization, or implantation.

heading_notes.heading: Cancer
notes: Some studies find associations with selected ovarian cancers, but the absolute cancer risk remains low.

Symptoms & causes.summary: Endometriosis is endometrial-like tissue growing outside the uterus, which can inflame pelvic tissue, cause pain, and affect fertility. Cyclic pelvic pain, severe cramps, painful sex, bowel or urination pain, heavy bleeding, infertility, fatigue, bloating, nausea, constipation/diarrhea may occur; some people have no symptoms. Seek care for persistent or severe pelvic pain that disrupts daily life. The cause is uncertain; theories include retrograde menstruation, cellular transformation, embryonic remnants, surgical implantation, immune factors, and cell transport. Early menstruation, short cycles, long/heavy periods, low body mass, blocked outflow, and family history may increase risk. Links to related procedures and tests. Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus; the page associates it with painful periods, pain during sex, fatigue and possible infertility.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: History, pelvic exam, ultrasound or MRI, and sometimes laparoscopy are used; imaging can identify cysts but may miss small lesions.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic exam
notes: A clinician may feel cysts or scar tissue, though a normal exam does not rule out endometriosis.

heading_notes.heading: Transvaginal ultrasound
notes: Ultrasound can identify ovarian endometriomas and other pelvic masses but may not show small superficial lesions.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on pain, fertility plans, disease severity, and preferences; options include pain medicines, hormones, surgery, and fertility care.

heading_notes.heading: Pain medicines
notes: NSAIDs may reduce pain and inflammation; they do not remove lesions.

heading_notes.heading: Hormone therapy
notes: Hormonal contraception, progestins, GnRH medicines, or other hormone-directed therapies suppress cycling and can relieve symptoms; symptoms may return after stopping.

heading_notes.heading: Conservative surgery
notes: Laparoscopy may remove or destroy visible endometriosis while preserving uterus/ovaries, especially when medicines fail or fertility is a goal.

heading_notes.heading: Fertility treatment
notes: Fertility medicines, insemination, or IVF may be considered with a specialist; surgery is individualized against conception prospects and procedural risks.

heading_notes.heading: Hysterectomy with removal of the ovaries
notes: This is a last-resort option for severe symptoms when childbearing is complete; it causes infertility/menopause and does not guarantee pain relief.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Heat, warm bathing, gentle activity, and pelvic-floor therapy may ease symptoms; pain tracking can identify patterns.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence for acupuncture and other complementary approaches is limited; discuss supplements and therapies with clinicians.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Persistent pain and fertility concerns can affect mood and relationships; support and counseling may help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring symptom timing, cycle/fertility history, prior treatments, medicines, and questions about pain and pregnancy plans.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Bring cycle-related symptom records and clarify whether pain relief, pregnancy, or both are priorities.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about pain timing, bleeding, sex, bowel/bladder symptoms, and fertility goals.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: It is endometrium-like tissue located outside the uterus and at sites distant from gynecologic organs. Abdominal-wall disease commonly causes a painful mass, often with pain worsening during menstruation; many cases follow cesarean or other uterine surgery. Thoracic disease can cause recurrent pneumothorax or coughing blood associated with menstruation.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Fecal incontinence - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Accidental stool leakage may occur with urgency before reaching a toilet or without awareness of rectal fullness; it can disrupt work, social life, and emotional wellbeing.
Diarrhea, constipation, and muscle or nerve injury are common contributors; evaluation and treatment can improve function and quality of life.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Urgency-related leakage is the urge to defecate without enough control to reach a toilet; passive leakage occurs without sensing the need to go.
Leakage may also occur while passing gas, and episodes can be temporary during diarrhea or chronic.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek assessment for recurrent leakage, emotional distress, disruption of daily activities, or withdrawal from social activities; embarrassment should not delay care.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Loose stool may overwhelm the rectum; hard stool can obstruct it and allow softer stool to seep around it.
Weak or injured anal, rectal, or pelvic-floor muscles may follow vaginal delivery, episiotomy, trauma, surgery, radiation, or aging.
Neurologic disease/injury can impair sensation and muscle coordination; structural contributors include rectal scarring/inflammation, rectal prolapse, hemorrhoids, and rectocele.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk depends on bowel consistency, pelvic/anal muscle integrity, neurologic health, age, childbirth injuries, and anorectal conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Leakage can limit activities and social participation and cause embarrassment or emotional strain.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Addressing bowel disorders, pelvic-floor health, and contributing conditions may reduce episodes; the source provides prevention guidance on the article page.

headings: Tests of rectal and anal function
What to expect from your doctor
What you can do in the meantime

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation covers symptom pattern, diet, medical history, anal/rectal examination, and neurologic function.
Rectal-function and imaging tests help identify impaired muscle coordination, structural disease, or other causes.

heading_notes.heading: Tests of rectal and anal function
notes: Anorectal manometry measures sphincter/rectal function and rectal capacity; balloon-expulsion testing assesses the ability to empty the rectum.

heading_notes.heading: Imaging tests
notes: Endoscopy can inspect bowel lining; endoscopic ultrasound, defecography (X-ray or MRI while evacuating), and anorectal MRI assess structure and function.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment aims to improve bowel consistency and anorectal control while addressing underlying conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Diet and lifestyle changes
notes: Gradually increase fiber, avoid foods and drinks that trigger diarrhea, stay hydrated, exercise, manage weight, and stop smoking.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Depending on the bowel problem, clinicians may use antidiarrheals, fiber supplements for constipation-related leakage, or laxatives to improve stool passage.

heading_notes.heading: Exercise and training
notes: Pelvic-floor and anal sphincter training, including Kegels and biofeedback, can improve awareness and control.

heading_notes.heading: Other treatments
notes: Additional approaches may be considered when diet, medicine, and exercise do not sufficiently control symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Sacral nerve stimulator
notes: Nerve stimulation is listed as a treatment option for selected patients whose symptoms persist.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Procedures may repair muscle damage or address structural causes when conservative treatment is inadequate.

heading_notes.heading: Self-care
notes: Care routines may include planned toileting and strategies to protect skin and manage leakage.

heading_notes.heading: Diaries
notes: Tracking bowel movements, food, symptoms, and episodes can help identify triggers and guide care.

heading_notes.heading: Skin care
notes: Gentle cleansing and protective skin care help reduce irritation from stool exposure.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Open discussion with clinicians and support can help address embarrassment and the effect on everyday life.

heading_notes.heading: If you have fecal incontinence
notes: This section focuses on practical management and support for living with symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Record symptoms, relevant health history, medicines, and questions before the visit.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about stool pattern, triggers, childbirth or surgery history, neurologic conditions, and symptom impact.

notes: Interim measures may include tracking triggers, maintaining hydration, and protecting irritated skin.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Female infertility-Female infertility - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Infertility generally means no pregnancy after a year of frequent unprotected sex; female factors contribute alone in about one third of cases and jointly with male factors in another third.
Cause may be a combination or remain unexplained; some couples conceive without treatment, and options depend on the cause.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Difficulty conceiving is the central sign; cycles longer than 35 days, shorter than 21 days, irregular, or absent can suggest ovulation problems. Other symptoms may be absent.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Under 35, evaluation is commonly considered after a year trying; ages 35–40 after six months; over 40, evaluation may be advised promptly.
Earlier assessment may be appropriate with known fertility concerns, irregular or painful periods, pelvic infection, repeated miscarriage, cancer treatment, or endometriosis.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Conception requires egg release, tubal pickup, sperm transport and fertilization, embryo travel, and implantation; disruption at any step can contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Female reproductive system
notes: The ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina form the reproductive tract involved in conception.

heading_notes.heading: Fertilization and implantation
notes: Sperm and egg unite in a tube; the early embryo travels to the uterus, develops through morula/blastocyst stages, and implants in the uterine lining.

heading_notes.heading: Ovulation disorders
notes: Irregular or absent ovulation is a leading cause; PCOS, hypothalamic/pituitary hormone disruption from stress or weight extremes, and diminished ovarian function are among contributors.

heading_notes.heading: Damage to fallopian tubes (tubal infertility)
notes: Tubal damage can block egg/sperm passage or embryo travel; prior infection, pelvic surgery, or other injury may be relevant.

heading_notes.heading: Endometriosis
notes: Endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus can inflame or scar pelvic structures and interfere with fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Uterine or cervical causes
notes: Structural or cervical problems can obstruct sperm passage or interfere with implantation and pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: Unexplained infertility
notes: Sometimes evaluation does not identify a single cause despite testing.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, smoking, substantial weight change, excessive exercise, alcohol or drug use, and reproductive or medical history can affect fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Some causes cannot be prevented; limiting tobacco and other harmful exposures and seeking care for reproductive infections may support fertility.

notes: Links to related procedures and tests.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Both partners should be evaluated; assessment includes detailed medical history and examination, with tests chosen for ovulation, egg reserve, hormones, uterine cavity, and tubal patency.

heading_notes.heading: Hysterosalpingography
notes: Contrast dye and X-ray show uterine cavity shape and whether fallopian tubes allow fluid to pass.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on cause, age, duration, and preferences; it may restore ovulation or anatomy or use assisted reproduction, with substantial time, cost, and emotional demands.

heading_notes.heading: Medications to restore fertility
notes: Ovulation medicines mimic or stimulate FSH/LH activity; options include clomiphene, injectable gonadotropins, metformin for insulin resistance/PCOS, and letrozole.

heading_notes.heading: Risks of fertility drugs
notes: Ovulation stimulation can increase the chance of multiple pregnancy and premature birth, especially with injectable gonadotropins.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery to restore fertility
notes: Selected procedures may correct tubal, uterine, or endometriosis-related problems.

heading_notes.heading: Reproductive assistance
notes: Assisted methods such as intrauterine insemination or IVF may help depending on diagnosis and treatment plan.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Fertility evaluation and treatment can be stressful; partner communication, counseling, and support resources may help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Prepare reproductive and medical history, cycle dates, prior testing/treatment, medicines, and questions; both partners may need to attend.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Record cycle patterns and questions about testing, options, treatment risks, costs, and timing.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about duration trying to conceive, cycle regularity, pregnancies, prior infections/surgeries, medications, and partner history.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Clinical Guideline #8: The fetus at risk for anemia—diagnosis and management — Fetal anemia
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Ultrasound Doppler measurement of middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) is recommended as the primary detection method; amniotic-fluid delta OD450 is not recommended for diagnosis. With MCA-PSV above 1.5 multiples of the median or hydrops, fetal blood sampling should be performed with preparation for intrauterine transfusion, with referral to an invasive fetal-therapy center; delivery is generally recommended at 37–38 weeks unless earlier indications arise.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Fetal macrosomia-Fetal macrosomia - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic
headings: Risks for the baby after birth
Talk with a healthcare professional first

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Fetal macrosomia means a newborn is substantially larger than average; before birth, clinicians estimate size because exact weight is known only after delivery.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: A large fundal-height measurement or excess amniotic fluid may raise suspicion, but neither confirms the baby's size.

heading_notes.heading: Fundal height
notes: Measuring from the pubic bone to the top of the uterus can suggest a larger-than-expected fetus when the measurement exceeds gestational expectations.

heading_notes.heading: Polyhydramnios
notes: More amniotic fluid than usual may accompany fetal macrosomia and prompt further evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Maternal diabetes and factors affecting fetal growth can contribute to excessive size.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk can be influenced by diabetes, prior large infant, excessive pregnancy weight gain, obesity before pregnancy, and longer gestation.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Large size may make vaginal delivery more difficult and increase birth injury and maternal delivery complications.

heading_notes.heading: Risks during labor and delivery
notes: Shoulder dystocia, birth trauma, prolonged labor, and cesarean delivery are concerns when the baby is very large.

heading_notes.heading: Risks for the baby after birth
notes: Newborn risks can include low blood sugar, injury, breathing problems, and later metabolic concerns.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Not all cases can be prevented; diabetes control, appropriate activity, and recommended pregnancy weight gain may reduce modifiable risks.

heading_notes.heading: Talk with a healthcare professional first
notes: Discuss safe activity and weight goals with the pregnancy-care team, particularly when medical conditions are present.

heading_notes.heading: Be active
notes: Regular pregnancy-safe activity may support healthy weight and glucose control.

heading_notes.heading: Gain pregnancy weight carefully
notes: Follow individualized weight-gain guidance based on pre-pregnancy health and pregnancy course.

heading_notes.heading: Manage diabetes
notes: Monitoring and managing diabetes helps reduce excessive fetal growth.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Fetal macrosomia-Fetal macrosomia - Diagnosis & treatment - Mayo Clinic

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Clinicians estimate fetal size from fundal height and ultrasound, but prenatal weight estimates have limits and cannot perfectly predict birth weight.

heading_notes.heading: Ultrasound
notes: Imaging estimates fetal size and growth; results are interpreted with other clinical information because measurements are not exact.

heading_notes.heading: Ongoing tests during pregnancy
notes: Additional monitoring may be used when diabetes or other factors increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Delivery planning weighs estimated fetal size, maternal diabetes, gestational age, prior birth history, and risks of vaginal versus cesarean delivery.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Discuss uncertainty in size estimates and delivery planning with the care team.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring pregnancy and diabetes records, prior birth outcomes, questions about monitoring, and delivery options.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Assessment may combine pelvic examination, imaging, blood tumor markers, and laboratory examination of removed tissue.

heading_notes.heading: Imaging tests
notes: Ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging help locate the tumor, estimate its extent, and guide surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Blood tests
notes: Tumor markers and other blood work can support diagnosis and help monitor response or recurrence.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Surgery removes or samples the tumor; the extent depends on spread and may be planned to preserve fertility when medically appropriate.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on tumor type, stage, and fertility goals; treatment may include surgery, chemotherapy, and less commonly radiation.

heading_notes.heading: Chemotherapy
notes: Drug treatment may be used after surgery or for disease that has spread or returned.

heading_notes.heading: Radiation therapy
notes: Radiation is considered in selected cases based on tumor type and clinical circumstances.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Prepare symptom history, previous imaging or surgery, medicines, and questions about tumor type, stage, fertility, and treatment effects.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Write down symptoms, health history, and questions before meeting the care team.

heading_notes.heading: Questions for your doctor
notes: Ask about tumor type and stage, whether fertility-preserving treatment is possible, treatment benefits and risks, and follow-up needs.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about symptoms, timing, menstrual history, family history, and prior diagnoses or treatment.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Complications that may affect your baby

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first recognized during pregnancy; it often has no noticeable symptoms and is identified through pregnancy screening.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Many people feel well; marked thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, or blurred vision may occur but are not reliable screening signs.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Discuss diabetes risk and screening timing with the pregnancy-care team; routine screening is part of prenatal care.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Pregnancy hormones can make insulin less effective; when the pancreas cannot produce enough insulin to meet increased needs, blood glucose rises.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk is higher with overweight/obesity, prior gestational diabetes or large infant, family history of type 2 diabetes, PCOS, and some demographic or metabolic factors.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Poorly controlled glucose can affect both pregnancy and future health, though monitoring and treatment lower risks.

heading_notes.heading: Complications that may affect your baby
notes: Potential effects include excessive fetal growth, early delivery, breathing or glucose problems after birth, and higher later-life risk of obesity or type 2 diabetes.

heading_notes.heading: Complications that may affect you
notes: Maternal risks include high blood pressure/preeclampsia, cesarean delivery, and increased future risk of gestational diabetes or type 2 diabetes.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Healthy activity, balanced eating, and weight management before and during pregnancy may lower risk but cannot prevent every case.

heading_notes.heading: News from Mayo Clinic
notes: Links to Mayo Clinic news articles and videos.

notes: Links to related procedures and tests.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Screening blood tests identify abnormal glucose during pregnancy; further glucose testing may confirm the diagnosis.

heading_notes.heading: Tests for gestational diabetes
notes: A glucose challenge test screens by measuring blood sugar after a sweet drink; an abnormal result is followed by a longer oral glucose tolerance test.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care focuses on blood-sugar control and monitoring fetal growth; some patients need medication in addition to lifestyle changes.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle changes
notes: A pregnancy-appropriate meal plan, regular physical activity, and clinician-guided weight goals support glucose control.

heading_notes.heading: Blood sugar monitoring
notes: Frequent home checks help determine whether glucose stays within the care team's targets.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Insulin is commonly used when lifestyle measures do not meet glucose targets; other medicines may be considered based on clinician guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Watching your baby closely
notes: Prenatal visits may include growth and wellbeing assessments, especially when glucose control is difficult.

heading_notes.heading: Follow-up after delivery
notes: Blood sugar often improves after birth, but postpartum testing is needed because future type 2 diabetes risk remains elevated.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Support from the care team and family can help with food planning, monitoring, and pregnancy concerns.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring glucose readings, food/activity notes, medication list, and questions about fetal monitoring and after-delivery testing.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track blood sugar and follow the individualized meal, activity, and medication plan.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about glucose records, diet, activity, symptoms, medication use, and pregnancy progress.

heading_notes.heading: News from Mayo Clinic
notes: Links to Mayo Clinic news articles and videos.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Granulosa cell tumor - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Granulosa cell tumors are uncommon ovarian tumors arising from hormone-producing support cells; many produce estrogen and some can recur after treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Types
notes: The main forms are adult and juvenile granulosa cell tumors, distinguished by age patterns and tumor features.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Possible signs include abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic or abdominal pain or swelling, and hormone-related changes; some tumors are found because of a mass.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The exact cause is not established; tumor cells develop genetic changes that support abnormal growth.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Specific preventable risk factors are not well established.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Estrogen production may cause endometrial overgrowth or bleeding; tumor growth or spread and late recurrence are concerns.

heading_notes.heading: Living with granulosa cell tumor?
notes: A patient community link is offered for peer support.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Heavy menstrual bleeding - Symptoms and causes
headings: Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, has been ranked among the best Obstetrics and Gynecology hospitals in the nation by U.S. News & World Report.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Heavy menstrual bleeding can interfere with daily life and may signal a treatable uterine, hormonal, or clotting problem.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Features include bleeding lasting more than a week, soaking pads or tampons rapidly, needing double protection or nighttime changes, passing large clots, and fatigue or breathlessness from anemia.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care for bleeding that disrupts life, requires frequent product changes, or causes possible anemia; urgent review is warranted for very heavy bleeding or weakness.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Potential causes include fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, ovulation/hormone disorders, bleeding conditions, some medicines, pregnancy complications, and less commonly cancer.

heading_notes.heading: Fibroid locations
notes: Fibroids may grow within the uterine wall, beneath the lining, or on the outer surface; location influences bleeding and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Uterine polyps
notes: Endometrial polyps are lining growths that can cause irregular or heavy bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Adenomyosis
notes: Adenomyosis can cause heavy bleeding and painful periods when lining-like tissue grows into uterine muscle.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk relates to reproductive age, ovulatory/hormonal conditions, uterine growths, bleeding disorders, and selected medications.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Ongoing heavy blood loss may lead to iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, weakness, and reduced quality of life.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Assessment includes menstrual history, physical/pelvic examination, blood work, imaging, and sometimes direct inspection or tissue sampling of the uterine cavity.

heading_notes.heading: Sonohysterography
notes: Fluid placed in the uterus improves ultrasound visualization of the cavity and can reveal polyps or other structural causes.

heading_notes.heading: Hysteroscopy
notes: A narrow lighted scope passed through the cervix lets the clinician inspect the uterine cavity and sometimes treat abnormalities.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Management depends on cause, severity, health history, and fertility plans; options include medicines and procedures.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Options may include hormonal contraception or progestin, a levonorgestrel IUD, tranexamic acid to reduce bleeding, and NSAIDs for bleeding and cramps.

heading_notes.heading: Procedures
notes: Procedures may remove polyps or fibroids, treat the uterine lining, or remove the uterus when other care fails and pregnancy is no longer desired.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Track bleeding amount and duration, cycles, symptoms, medicines, and pregnancy goals; bring questions about tests and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Record product use, clotting, pain, cycle dates, and effects on activity.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about bleeding pattern, last period, pregnancy possibility, contraception, medicines, and family or personal bleeding history.
