Symptoms & causes.page_title: High blood pressure (hypertension): Controlling this common health problem-High blood pressure (hypertension) - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Primary hypertension, also called essential hypertension

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Hypertension is persistently elevated pressure in arteries and usually causes no symptoms; measurement is needed to detect it.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Most people with high blood pressure have no warning symptoms, even when readings are dangerously high.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Regular measurement is important; emergency symptoms such as chest pain, severe shortness of breath, neurologic changes, or severe headache need urgent assessment.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Primary hypertension develops gradually without one identifiable cause; secondary hypertension results from another condition or medicine.

heading_notes.heading: Primary hypertension, also called essential hypertension
notes: This common form develops over years through multiple influences rather than a single cause.

heading_notes.heading: Secondary hypertension
notes: Possible contributors include kidney or endocrine disease, sleep apnea, congenital blood-vessel problems, and certain medicines or substances.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, family history, excess weight, inactivity, high-sodium diet, tobacco, alcohol, stress, and some chronic conditions increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Uncontrolled pressure can damage blood vessels and organs, raising risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, vision problems, aneurysm, and cognitive decline.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Diagnosis relies on repeated accurate readings; additional tests assess organ effects and possible secondary causes.

heading_notes.heading: Blood pressure measurement
notes: A cuff measures systolic and diastolic pressure; correct cuff size, positioning, rest, and repeated readings improve accuracy.

heading_notes.heading: Tests
notes: Blood and urine tests, ECG, and other assessments may look for underlying causes or heart/kidney effects.

heading_notes.heading: Taking your blood pressure at home
notes: Home monitoring can show trends between visits; use a validated cuff and share readings with the clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Lifestyle changes are foundational; medication is chosen based on pressure level, cardiovascular risk, other conditions, and response.

heading_notes.heading: Medications
notes: Common classes include diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, and other agents selected for the individual.

heading_notes.heading: Other medicines sometimes used to treat high blood pressure
notes: Additional drug classes may be used when first choices are unsuitable or pressure remains high.

heading_notes.heading: Treating resistant hypertension
notes: Persistent elevation despite several medicines may prompt review of adherence, measurement, interfering substances, and secondary causes.

heading_notes.heading: High blood pressure during pregnancy
notes: Pregnancy-related hypertension requires specialized monitoring and treatment to protect both pregnant patient and fetus.

heading_notes.heading: Potential future treatments
notes: Research continues into additional approaches for difficult-to-control hypertension.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Self care
notes: Limit sodium, follow a heart-healthy diet, exercise, maintain healthy weight, limit alcohol, avoid tobacco, and take prescribed medicines consistently.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Discuss supplements and complementary products because some affect blood pressure or interact with medication.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Ongoing monitoring and treatment plans can help people manage a usually symptom-free chronic condition.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring a list of readings, medicines, supplements, relevant health history, and questions.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask whether home measurement is appropriate and bring the cuff or records if requested.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about readings, medicines, diet, activity, smoking, sleep, family history, and symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do in the meantime
notes: Continue prescribed medicines and record readings; do not stop treatment without medical advice.

notes: Links to Mayo Clinic news articles and videos.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Hirsutism is coarse, dark hair growth in a male-pattern distribution in women; the amount and emotional impact vary.

heading_notes.heading: Hirsutism
notes: The page distinguishes unwanted terminal hair growth from fine body hair and notes that androgen activity is commonly involved.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Coarse hair may appear on the face, chest, abdomen, back, or thighs; acne, scalp hair thinning, or voice/body changes may accompany androgen excess.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Rapid onset, rapid progression, or signs of virilization warrant prompt medical assessment.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: PCOS is a common cause; other possibilities include adrenal or ovarian hormone disorders, certain medicines, and rarely androgen-producing tumors. Some cases have no identified cause.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Family background, PCOS, obesity/insulin resistance, and conditions that raise androgen levels can increase likelihood.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: The condition may cause emotional distress; an underlying hormone disorder may have additional health effects.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Many causes cannot be prevented; managing contributing conditions may help reduce symptoms.

notes: Approach depends on the cause, hair-growth rate, pregnancy plans, and personal preferences; medication takes months to reduce new growth, while removal methods address existing hair.

notes: Hormonal contraceptives can reduce androgen effects; antiandrogen medicines may be added when appropriate, with pregnancy prevention needed because of fetal risk.

notes: Laser hair removal and electrolysis can reduce hair; selection depends on skin/hair characteristics and potential side effects.

notes: Shaving, waxing, plucking, depilatory creams, or bleaching can manage hair temporarily; methods differ in irritation and regrowth.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Human papillomavirus is a common group of viruses; some types cause skin or genital warts, while persistent high-risk types can lead to cancers.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Many infections cause no symptoms and clear without treatment; visible warts vary by site and appearance, while cervical precancer/cancer may be symptom-free early.

heading_notes.heading: Common warts
notes: Raised rough growths often occur on hands or fingers and may be dark-speckled.

heading_notes.heading: Plantar warts
notes: Hard growths on the soles can be painful with walking and may grow inward under pressure.

heading_notes.heading: Flat warts
notes: Small, smooth, slightly raised lesions may appear in groups, commonly on the face or legs.

heading_notes.heading: Female genital warts
notes: Soft bumps may be flat or raised and occur on the vulva, vagina, cervix, or around the anus.

heading_notes.heading: Male genital warts
notes: Genital lesions may occur on the penis, scrotum, groin, or around the anus.

heading_notes.heading: Cervical cancer
notes: High-risk HPV is the principal cause of cervical cancer; screening detects precancerous changes before symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek assessment for new or changing genital lesions, abnormal cervical screening, or symptoms that concern you.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: HPV spreads through close skin-to-skin contact, often during vaginal, anal, or oral sex; infection can occur without visible warts.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: New or multiple partners, weakened immunity, and unprotected sexual contact increase exposure risk; infection can occur with one partner.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Some strains cause warts; persistent oncogenic strains can lead to cervical, vaginal, vulvar, anal, penile, or throat cancers.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Vaccination, routine cervical screening, and barrier protection reduce—but do not eliminate—risk.

heading_notes.heading: Genital warts
notes: Wart-causing HPV types differ from the main cancer-causing types; treatment removes lesions but may not eradicate the virus.

heading_notes.heading: HPV vaccines
notes: Vaccination protects against several wart- and cancer-associated types and works best before exposure.

heading_notes.heading: News from Mayo Clinic
notes: Links to Mayo Clinic news articles and videos.

headings: Treatment for HPV in the cervix
From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: HPV testing and cervical screening identify high-risk infection or abnormal cervical cells; visible warts are often diagnosed by examination.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: There is no medicine that removes HPV itself; care treats warts or precancerous/cancerous tissue, while many infections resolve without intervention.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Topical prescription medicines may help clear certain external warts; the clinician selects treatment by location and type.

heading_notes.heading: Surgical and other procedures
notes: Cryotherapy, acids, electrosurgery, laser, or surgical removal may be used for warts or abnormal tissue.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment for HPV in the cervix
notes: Abnormal cervical cells may be monitored or removed with procedures such as excision or ablation, depending on severity and risk.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring screening results, lesion history, vaccination status, medicines, and questions about partner communication and follow-up.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Abdominal and perineal examination plus ultrasonography can identify a bulging hymen with hematocolpos; MRI is recommended when the diagnosis or another obstructing anomaly is uncertain. heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Cervical insufficiency means the cervix opens or shortens too early in pregnancy, potentially leading to second-trimester loss or premature birth.

heading_notes.heading: Female reproductive system
notes: The cervix is the lower opening of the uterus into the vagina and normally remains closed during pregnancy until labor.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Often there are no symptoms before cervical change; possible signs include pelvic pressure, backache, mild cramps, vaginal discharge changes, or spotting.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior painless second-trimester loss or early birth, cervical surgery/trauma, congenital uterine or cervical differences, and some connective-tissue disorders may raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Early cervical opening can lead to pregnancy loss, membrane rupture, infection, or premature delivery.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Prior history may prompt closer cervical-length monitoring and preventive treatment in a later pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Infertility concerns a couple's difficulty achieving pregnancy; causes may involve either partner, both partners, or remain unexplained.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Often the only sign is inability to conceive; cycle irregularity may signal ovulation difficulty in women, while male symptoms may be absent.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Evaluation timing depends on age and history; earlier assessment is appropriate with known reproductive problems or risk factors.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Conception requires ovulation, sperm production and delivery, fertilization, embryo transport, and implantation; disruption at any step may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Fertilization and implantation
notes: The sperm and egg meet, the embryo travels through the tube, and implantation occurs in the uterine lining.

heading_notes.heading: Male reproductive system
notes: Sperm production and transport involve the testes, ducts, accessory glands, and penis.

heading_notes.heading: Female reproductive system
notes: Ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina support ovulation, fertilization, transport, and pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: Causes of male infertility
notes: Contributors include impaired sperm production or quality, obstruction, hormonal problems, illness, medications, and lifestyle or environmental factors.

heading_notes.heading: Causes of female infertility
notes: Ovulation disorders, tubal damage, endometriosis, uterine/cervical factors, and age-related egg changes are common categories.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, smoking, alcohol/drug use, weight extremes, chronic illness, and reproductive infections or surgeries may affect fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Some causes cannot be prevented; avoiding tobacco/drugs, limiting alcohol, maintaining health, and reducing STI exposure may support reproductive health.

heading_notes.heading: Couples
notes: Shared evaluation helps identify combined factors and align treatment choices.

heading_notes.heading: Men
notes: Male evaluation may include semen analysis and targeted examination or hormone testing.

heading_notes.heading: Women
notes: Female evaluation may assess ovulation, ovarian reserve, tubes, and uterine anatomy.

What to expect from your doctor
Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, has been ranked among the best Obstetrics and Gynecology hospitals in the nation by U.S. News & World Report.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Both partners may need medical history, physical examination, and targeted testing; the work-up is tailored to likely causes.

heading_notes.heading: Tests for men
notes: Semen analysis assesses sperm amount and quality; hormone, genetic, or imaging tests may be added.

heading_notes.heading: Tests for women
notes: Testing may assess ovulation, ovarian reserve, hormone levels, tubal patency, and uterine structure.

heading_notes.heading: Sonohysterography
notes: Saline-enhanced ultrasound outlines the uterine cavity and can reveal structural abnormalities.

heading_notes.heading: Hysteroscopy
notes: A scope passed through the cervix directly examines the uterine cavity.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Options depend on diagnosis and may treat a specific cause, use fertility medicines, surgery, insemination, or assisted reproductive technology.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment for men
notes: Treatment may address hormonal or sexual problems, infection, obstruction, or sperm retrieval.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment for women
notes: Care may stimulate ovulation, correct selected structural conditions, or use assisted reproduction.

heading_notes.heading: Assisted reproductive technology
notes: ART combines eggs and sperm outside the body or supports fertilization/embryo transfer; choices depend on the couple's diagnosis.

heading_notes.heading: In vitro fertilization
notes: IVF involves ovarian stimulation, egg retrieval, fertilization in a laboratory, and transfer of an embryo to the uterus.

heading_notes.heading: ICSI
notes: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection places one sperm into an egg and may be used for significant sperm-related infertility or prior fertilization failure.

heading_notes.heading: Complications of treatment
notes: Fertility care can involve multiple pregnancy, ovarian hyperstimulation, ectopic pregnancy, emotional burden, and financial/time costs.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Counseling, partner communication, peer support, and clear information may help during uncertain treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Managing stress during treatment
notes: Stress-management approaches and support can help with the emotional demands of testing and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Managing emotional effects of the outcome
notes: Coping support may be useful whether treatment succeeds, ends, or the couple considers other family-building options.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring both partners' histories, prior results, medicines, and questions about options and likely timelines.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about test purpose, success rates, risks, costs, and alternatives; keep records of cycle timing and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about pregnancy history, duration trying, sexual health, cycles, prior illness, surgery, and medications.

heading_notes.heading: Questions for couples
notes: Discuss shared priorities, testing, treatment sequence, risks, and financial/emotional commitments.

heading_notes.heading: Questions for men
notes: Ask about semen testing, possible causes, treatments, and implications for future fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Questions for the woman
notes: Ask about ovulation, ovarian reserve, uterine/tubal evaluation, treatment choices, and pregnancy risks.

findings: Assesses endometrial thickness/polyp, fibroid, adenomyosis pattern, ovarian morphology/cyst, antral follicles, uterine anomaly, retained material, and pelvic mass.

tests.specimen_or_method: High-frequency transvaginal pelvic imaging with Doppler when indicated
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: 4.8-cm complex adnexal lesion with solid vascular mural nodule and free pelvic fluid; alternatively, focal endometrial polyp/fibroid/adenomyosis features described with dimensions.
tests.interpretation: Complexity, vascularity, and associated fluid increase concern and guide specialist work-up; morphology is not histology.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no adnexal mass, no free fluid, and no focal endometrial lesion visualized within technical limits.

findings: MRI can define adenomyosis, deep endometriosis, complex Müllerian anomaly, scar defect, or indeterminate mass when ultrasound is insufficient.
pertinent_negatives: Normal MRI does not exclude superficial endometriosis or functional causes of bleeding.

tests.specimen_or_method: Multiplanar soft-tissue MRI; contrast only when appropriate to context
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: T2-hypointense junctional-zone thickening with myometrial cysts (adenomyosis pattern), deep infiltrating endometriosis, indeterminate adnexal lesion, or local tumor extension characterized.
tests.interpretation: Problem-solving/staging modality after or alongside ultrasound; report must describe location, size, invasion, and involved structures.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no definite deep invasion, complex fistula tract, or extra-organ extension identified.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Lichen planus is an inflammatory condition that can affect skin, mouth, nails, scalp, or genital tissue; it is not an infection.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Itchy, flat-topped purple or reddish bumps may occur on skin; oral disease can cause white lacy patches, soreness, or erosions; genital involvement may cause irritation or pain.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek assessment for persistent rash, mouth/genital sores, pain, or symptoms affecting eating, urination, or sexual activity.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The immune system appears to contribute; the exact trigger is unknown. Some cases are associated with medicines, hepatitis C, or other exposures.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Middle age and certain medical or medication histories may be associated, depending on the form and body site.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Persistent inflammation may scar genital tissue, affect oral comfort, or cause hair loss when scalp follicles are involved.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Diagnosis is often based on examination; skin biopsy or tests for associated conditions may be used when the appearance is uncertain.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment aims to reduce itching and inflammation; choice depends on body site and severity, and some cases resolve over time.

heading_notes.heading: Corticosteroids
notes: Topical or systemic corticosteroids reduce inflammation; route and duration depend on affected area and severity.

heading_notes.heading: Oral anti-infections drugs
notes: Selected oral medicines may help when inflammation is widespread or difficult to control.

heading_notes.heading: Immune response medicines
notes: Immune-modulating medicines may be considered for severe or persistent disease.

heading_notes.heading: Antihistamines
notes: Antihistamines may reduce itching or help sleep when symptoms are disruptive.

heading_notes.heading: Light therapy
notes: Phototherapy can help some widespread skin cases.

heading_notes.heading: Retinoids
notes: Retinoid medicines may be used for selected cases but can have important side effects and pregnancy restrictions.

heading_notes.heading: Dealing with triggers
notes: Review medicines and associated conditions with a clinician if a trigger is suspected.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Gentle skin care and avoiding irritants or scratching can reduce additional irritation.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence for complementary products is limited; discuss safety and interactions with a clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring a medication list, symptom timeline, affected-site details, and questions about scarring and treatment effects.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Note itch/pain patterns, exposures, and medicines; ask about self-care for the involved site.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about onset, affected areas, medication use, hepatitis C or other conditions, and symptom triggers.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Lichen sclerosus - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that often affects genital or anal skin and can cause fragile, itchy, pale patches.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Genital symptoms may include itching, discomfort, easy bruising/tearing, pain with sex or urination, and white thin patches; some people have no symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Lichen sclerosus
notes: The condition can affect anyone but is more common in women after menopause; it may occur outside genital skin as well.

heading_notes.heading: Lichen sclerosus in genital area
notes: Vulvar/anal skin may scar or change shape over time; penile involvement can affect foreskin and urination.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Get evaluation for persistent genital itching, pain, skin changes, or sores.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause is uncertain; autoimmune factors, hormones, and genetic susceptibility may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Postmenopausal status, autoimmune disease, family predisposition, and prior skin injury may be associated.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Scarring can narrow openings or alter genital anatomy; ongoing inflammation can impair sexual or urinary function, and a small cancer risk warrants follow-up.

notes: Links to related health topics and articles.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment controls symptoms and inflammation and helps prevent scarring; long-term follow-up is often needed.

heading_notes.heading: Medicated ointments
notes: Prescription corticosteroid ointment is commonly used, with an initial intensive course followed by maintenance as directed.

heading_notes.heading: Circumcision
notes: For penile disease that does not respond to medicine or causes foreskin problems, circumcision may be considered.

heading_notes.heading: Clinical trials

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies

Symptoms & causes.summary: Vulvar high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (VIN usual type) is associated with human papillomavirus; ACOG describes VIN as a premalignant condition. Symptoms & causes.page_title: Menopause - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Menopause is the point when 12 months have passed without a menstrual period; the transition can cause symptoms as ovarian hormone production declines.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Hot flashes, night sweats, sleep and mood changes, vaginal/urinary symptoms, and changes in sexual comfort may occur; timing and severity vary.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Discuss disruptive symptoms or bleeding after menopause; postmenopausal bleeding needs evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Natural menopause follows declining ovarian function; surgery, cancer treatment, or ovarian insufficiency can cause earlier menopause.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age is the main factor for natural menopause; smoking, family history, chemotherapy/radiation, and ovarian surgery may affect timing.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Menstrual cramps-Menstrual cramps - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Menstrual cramps are throbbing or cramping lower-abdominal pain around menstruation; primary cramps occur without another pelvic disorder, while secondary cramps stem from disease.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Pain may radiate to the lower back or thighs and can include nausea, loose stools, headache, or dizziness; severity ranges from mild to disabling.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care when cramps worsen, disrupt daily activities, or begin later in life; sudden severe pain warrants urgent evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Prostaglandins trigger uterine contractions; higher levels are linked to stronger cramps. Secondary causes include endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, and cervical narrowing.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Younger age, early menstruation, heavy bleeding, smoking, and family history may increase primary cramp risk; pelvic disease raises secondary-cramp likelihood.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Pain can interfere with school, work, sleep, and activity; secondary causes may carry additional fertility or pelvic-health effects.

heading_notes.heading: Associated Procedures
notes: Links to related procedures and tests.

notes: Record when cramps occur, what improves them, and whether pain affects daily activities.

notes: Expect questions about cycle pattern, pain onset and severity, sexual/reproductive history, and other pelvic symptoms.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Miscarriage - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Miscarriage is loss of a pregnancy before 20 weeks; many early losses occur because an embryo cannot develop normally.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Vaginal spotting or bleeding, fluid/tissue passage, and lower abdominal or back cramping may occur; symptoms can vary.

heading_notes.heading: When to seek emergency care
notes: Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, or feeling faint needs urgent medical attention; contact a pregnancy-care professional for bleeding or pain.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Many losses involve random chromosome problems; maternal health conditions and other factors can contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Irregular genes or chromosomes
notes: Abnormal chromosome number or structure can prevent normal embryonic development; this is often not caused by an inherited problem.

heading_notes.heading: Maternal health conditions
notes: Uncontrolled diabetes, thyroid or hormonal disorders, uterine/cervical problems, and some infections may raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: What does NOT cause miscarriage
notes: Ordinary exercise, sex, work, or common emotional stress generally do not cause miscarriage.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Risk increases with age and may be affected by prior losses, smoking, alcohol/drug use, chronic disease, and uterine/cervical conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Incomplete miscarriage or infection may require treatment; repeated losses may need evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Many losses cannot be prevented; managing chronic conditions, avoiding tobacco/alcohol/drugs, and prenatal care support a healthy pregnancy.

notes: Links to related health topics and articles.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Options depend on symptoms and clinical findings: expectant management, medicines to help pass tissue, or a procedure to empty the uterus.

heading_notes.heading: Threatened miscarriage
notes: Bleeding with a closed cervix and ongoing pregnancy may be monitored; follow care-team instructions and report worsening symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Miscarriage
notes: If loss is confirmed, clinicians discuss waiting, medication, or uterine evacuation according to medical need and patient preference.

heading_notes.heading: Physical recovery
notes: Bleeding and cramping generally lessen over time; follow guidance about activity, infection signs, and follow-up.

heading_notes.heading: Future pregnancies
notes: Many people have a later healthy pregnancy; evaluation may be offered after repeated losses or when a specific risk is identified.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Grief responses vary; counseling, trusted support, and pregnancy-loss groups can help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring pregnancy dates, symptoms, prior losses, medicines, and questions about treatment and future pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about warning signs, follow-up, and when to try again if desired.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about bleeding, pain, pregnancy dating, prior pregnancies, and medical conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Related
notes: Links to related health topics and articles.

notes: Links to related procedures and tests.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

findings: Pregnancy-targeted ultrasound is chosen to assess viability, location, fetal number/anatomy, placental location/invasion markers, amniotic fluid, growth, Doppler findings, or cervical length as applicable.
Transvaginal imaging is particularly useful for early pregnancy location, cervix, placenta previa, and lower-pelvic anatomy.
pertinent_negatives: No intrauterine gestation at a discriminatory hCG level is concerning but must be interpreted with dates, assay, and repeat testing; a single scan should not be used alone to declare nonviability.

severity_or_range.intermediate: Persistent abnormality or multiple markers.
severity_or_range.high_or_advanced: Clear anatomic, viability, perfusion, growth, or placental abnormality requiring urgent specialist-directed assessment.

tests.specimen_or_method: Transvaginal early-pregnancy or transabdominal obstetric imaging
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: gestational location/viability, crown–rump length or biometry, placental location, fluid volume, fetal anatomy, and cervical length documented; abnormality described with measurements and Doppler if relevant.
tests.interpretation: Supports pregnancy location, fetal/placental assessment, or cervical assessment; serial imaging may be needed.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: intrauterine gestation with expected interval growth; no previa, major surveyed anomaly, or abnormal fluid finding at that scan.

pertinent_negatives: Not first-line when ultrasound answers the clinical question.

tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: T2-hypointense junctional-zone thickening with myometrial cysts (adenomyosis pattern), deep infiltrating endometriosis, indeterminate adnexal lesion, or local tumor extension characterized.
tests.interpretation: Problem-solving/staging modality after or alongside ultrasound; report must describe location, size, invasion, and involved structures.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no definite deep invasion, complex fistula tract, or extra-organ extension identified.

tests.test_name: Nine-quadrant abdominal examination with PQRSTU pain history
tests.specimen_or_method: Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation, and PQRSTU: provoking/palliating factors, quality, region/radiation, severity, timing, understanding/impact
tests.example_indicative_result: Example: sudden unilateral lower-quadrant pain (8/10), radiating to shoulder, worse with movement, with focal guarding; or right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea/pruritus depending on disorder.
tests.interpretation: Focal tenderness/guarding, distension, mass, hepatomegaly, or peritoneal signs change urgency and imaging/laboratory selection.

tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no visible lesion/discharge, no cervical-motion tenderness, no adnexal mass/tenderness, and no uterine enlargement within examination limits.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: ACOG, Management of Acute Obstructive Uterovaginal Anomalies — Mullerian anomalies
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Müllerian anomalies result from abnormal embryologic development of the reproductive tract and can involve the uterus, cervix, or vagina. Obstructive anomalies may present with primary amenorrhea, cyclic or persistent pelvic pain, and a pelvic mass from retained menstrual blood.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation commonly uses pelvic ultrasonography; MRI is recommended when the anatomy is uncertain or an obstructed uterine or vaginal anomaly is suspected. Management depends on the specific anomaly and may require planned surgical intervention; ACOG emphasizes complete anatomic evaluation and care by experienced gynecologic providers.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: ACOG, Multiple Pregnancy — Multiple gestation
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Fertility drugs that induce ovulation can release more than one egg and lead to twins, triplets, or more. Compared with singleton pregnancy, multiple pregnancy may cause more severe morning sickness or breast tenderness and faster weight gain; preterm birth is the most common complication.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: ACOG, Multiple Pregnancy — Multiple gestation
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Most multiple pregnancies are diagnosed by ultrasound; early ultrasound determines chorionicity and amnionicity. Care generally includes more frequent prenatal visits and serial ultrasound examinations; monochorionic pregnancies require monitoring for complications such as twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

heading_notes.heading: Ovarian cancer

notes: Persistent abdominal bloating, pelvic/abdominal discomfort, feeling full quickly, and urinary urgency/frequency are common warning patterns; unusual bleeding may also occur.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation may include pelvic examination, imaging, blood tests such as CA-125, and surgery/biopsy to confirm cancer and determine stage.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic exam
notes: A clinician examines pelvic organs for masses or changes; an exam alone cannot establish cancer.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care is individualized by cancer type and stage and may include surgery, chemotherapy, targeted/hormone therapy, immunotherapy, and symptom-focused care.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Operations may remove one or both ovaries, tubes, uterus, nearby tissues, and visible tumor; fertility-sparing options may be possible for selected early disease.

heading_notes.heading: Chemotherapy
notes: Drug therapy may be given before or after surgery or for recurrent/advanced disease.

heading_notes.heading: Targeted therapy
notes: Medicines attack specific cancer-cell pathways and may be selected using tumor features.

heading_notes.heading: Hormone therapy
notes: Hormone-blocking treatment may be useful for selected tumor types.

heading_notes.heading: Immunotherapy
notes: Immune-based medicines may be considered for particular advanced cancers.

heading_notes.heading: Supportive (palliative) care
notes: Symptom relief and quality-of-life support can be provided alongside cancer treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Information, close relationships, counseling, and peer support can help people manage diagnosis and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring symptoms, medical/family history, medicines, and questions about stage, fertility, treatment, and side effects.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about diagnosis confirmation, treatment goals, alternatives, and how care may affect future fertility.

heading_notes.heading: Questions to ask your doctor
notes: Ask what type and stage of cancer is present, what treatment is recommended, expected benefits/risks, and what follow-up is needed.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Ovarian cysts - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Ovarian cysts are fluid-filled or solid pockets in or on an ovary; many are common, functional, and resolve without treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Female reproductive system
notes: Ovaries release eggs and produce hormones; the diagram situates them beside the uterus and fallopian tubes.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Most cysts cause no symptoms; larger or complicated cysts may cause pelvic pain, fullness, bloating, or pressure.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Sudden severe pelvic pain, pain with fever/vomiting, or signs of shock require urgent assessment because rupture or torsion may occur.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Many cysts form during the menstrual cycle; other types arise from endometriosis or abnormal cell growth.

heading_notes.heading: Follicular cyst
notes: A follicle that does not release an egg or close properly may continue growing and form a fluid-filled cyst.

heading_notes.heading: Corpus luteum cyst
notes: After egg release, the follicle sac may close and collect fluid or blood, enlarging into a cyst.

heading_notes.heading: Functional cysts
notes: Follicular and corpus luteum cysts are cycle-related and often disappear spontaneously within a few menstrual cycles.

heading_notes.heading: Other cysts
notes: Endometriomas, dermoid cysts, and cystadenomas differ in tissue origin and behavior; most are benign but may grow or cause complications.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Hormonal medicines, pregnancy, endometriosis, prior ovarian cysts, and severe pelvic infection may increase likelihood.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Large cysts may rupture or twist the ovary (torsion), causing sudden pain and potentially affecting ovarian blood supply.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: There is no certain prevention; regular pelvic assessment and attention to new symptoms can help identify changes.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: It occurs when ovarian tissue remains after bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with or without hysterectomy, and may produce pelvic pain or a pelvic mass. Reported risk factors for incomplete ovarian removal include endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, multiple prior surgeries, and pelvic adhesions; presentations include chronic pelvic pain or an asymptomatic pelvic mass.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Overactive bladder - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Overactive bladder is a symptom pattern involving sudden urgency, often with frequent urination and nighttime urination, with or without urge leakage.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Urgency, frequent daytime voiding, nocturia, and urge incontinence may occur; symptoms can affect sleep, work, and social activity.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek assessment when urgency/frequency disrupts daily life or is accompanied by pain, blood in urine, or difficulty emptying.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Involuntary bladder-muscle contractions create urgency; neurologic disorders, bladder irritation, infection, obstruction, or other conditions may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: How a healthy bladder works
notes: The kidneys produce urine, which travels to the bladder; the bladder stores it until coordinated muscle contraction and sphincter relaxation allow urination.

heading_notes.heading: Female urinary system
notes: Female urinary anatomy includes kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.

heading_notes.heading: Male urinary system
notes: Male urinary anatomy includes kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra, and prostate-related structures.

heading_notes.heading: Involuntary bladder contractions
notes: Urgency can occur when bladder muscles contract before the bladder is full.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, neurologic disease, diabetes, urinary tract changes, prior pelvic surgery, and bladder outlet obstruction can increase likelihood.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Sleep disruption, falls during nighttime trips, anxiety, and reduced participation in activities may result.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Healthy fluid habits, pelvic-floor training, and addressing contributing conditions may reduce symptoms.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Overactive bladder - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation includes symptom/voiding history, physical examination, and urine testing; further assessment checks bladder emptying and function.

heading_notes.heading: Tests of bladder function
notes: Bladder diary, residual urine measurement, urine tests, and urodynamic studies may clarify capacity, contractions, and emptying.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment often begins with behavioral changes and pelvic-floor training, then medicines or procedures if symptoms continue.

heading_notes.heading: Behavioral therapies
notes: Bladder training, scheduled voiding, urgency-suppression techniques, and pelvic-floor exercises can improve control.

heading_notes.heading: Female pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic-floor muscles support bladder and pelvic organs and help control urine flow.

heading_notes.heading: Male pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic-floor muscles contribute to urinary control and can be trained.

heading_notes.heading: Medications
notes: Antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist medicines can relax bladder muscle; side effects and other conditions guide selection.

heading_notes.heading: Bladder injections
notes: Botulinum toxin injected into bladder muscle may reduce urgency, with possible temporary retention or need for catheterization.

heading_notes.heading: Nerve stimulation
notes: Nerve-based therapies can alter signals involved in bladder urgency.

heading_notes.heading: Sacral nerve stimulator
notes: An implanted device modulates sacral nerve signals for selected persistent cases.

heading_notes.heading: Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (PTNS)
notes: Repeated stimulation near the ankle influences bladder nerve pathways.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Surgery is reserved for severe cases that have not responded to other treatments.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Manage caffeine/alcohol and fluid timing, maintain healthy weight, address constipation, and use bladder training.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence is limited for many complementary treatments; review options with a clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Planning access to toilets and support can reduce the social burden.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring a bladder diary, medicine list, symptom history, and questions about treatment benefits and side effects.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track fluids, voiding times, urgency/leakage episodes, and triggers.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about frequency, nighttime urination, leakage, fluid intake, medicines, and neurologic/urinary history.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Pelvic organ prolapse - Symptoms and causes
headings: Get the latest health information from Mayo Clinic delivered to your inbox.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when weakened pelvic support allows organs such as the bladder, uterus, or rectum to descend into or through the vagina.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: A vaginal bulge, pelvic pressure/heaviness, urinary or bowel difficulty, and discomfort with sex may occur; some people have no symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Get the latest health information from Mayo Clinic delivered to your inbox.
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Pregnancy and vaginal birth can stretch pelvic support; aging, menopause-related tissue changes, and chronic pressure can contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Vaginal childbirth, older age, obesity, chronic cough/constipation, heavy lifting, prior pelvic surgery, and connective-tissue weakness are associated risks.

notes: Pelvic examination while bearing down can identify prolapse and affected organs; evaluation may include bladder or bowel tests.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on symptoms and severity; options include observation, pelvic-floor therapy, pessary support, or surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Medications
notes: Estrogen therapy may improve vaginal tissue in selected postmenopausal patients but does not correct prolapse.

heading_notes.heading: Physical therapy
notes: Pelvic-floor exercises and therapist-guided training may improve support and symptom control.

heading_notes.heading: Pessaries
notes: A removable vaginal device supports pelvic organs; fitting, cleaning, and follow-up are important.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Surgical repair rebuilds support; approach depends on organ, symptoms, sexual goals, and recurrence risk.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Perimenopause - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Perimenopause is the transition before menopause, when hormone levels fluctuate and menstrual cycles and symptoms change.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Periods may become irregular; hot flashes, sleep disruption, mood changes, vaginal dryness, and libido changes may occur.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek advice for severe symptoms, very heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods, or bleeding after sex.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Changing ovarian hormone production drives the transition; it continues until menopause is reached.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age and individual ovarian reserve influence timing; smoking or certain treatments may bring transition earlier.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Irregular heavy bleeding may need evaluation; declining estrogen contributes to bone loss and genitourinary symptoms.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Peripartum cardiomyopathy - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is a rare weakening of the heart muscle arising late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery; it can cause heart failure.

heading_notes.heading: Types
notes: The page describes cardiomyopathy by the heart-muscle changes and timing around pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: Dilated cardiomyopathy
notes: The heart's main pumping chamber enlarges and weakens, reducing its ability to pump blood.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Shortness of breath, fatigue, swelling in legs/feet, cough, chest discomfort, palpitations, and difficulty lying flat may occur.

heading_notes.heading: When to seek care
notes: Contact a clinician for new or worsening breathlessness, swelling, or fatigue around pregnancy/postpartum.

heading_notes.heading: When to seek emergency care
notes: Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting, or rapidly worsening symptoms require emergency care.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The precise cause is unknown; pregnancy-related cardiovascular strain and other biologic factors may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Multiple pregnancy, preeclampsia/high blood pressure, older maternal age, obesity, and prior or family heart disease can raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Heart failure, dangerous arrhythmia, blood clots, valve problems, and death are possible in severe disease.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: There is no sure prevention; identifying cardiovascular risks and promptly reporting symptoms may improve care.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation includes examination, blood tests, echocardiography, ECG, chest imaging, and sometimes genetic or other testing to assess heart function and exclude alternatives.

heading_notes.heading: Blood tests
notes: Blood tests assess heart strain and other causes of symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Echocardiogram
notes: Ultrasound of the heart measures chamber size, pumping function, and valve function.

heading_notes.heading: Other tests
notes: ECG, chest X-ray, and additional imaging help assess rhythm, congestion, and heart structure.

heading_notes.heading: Genetic testing
notes: Testing may be considered when inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment follows heart-failure principles while accounting for pregnancy and breastfeeding; severity guides medicines, devices, or advanced care.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Diuretics, beta blockers, and other heart-failure medicines may be used, with pregnancy/lactation safety guiding selection.

heading_notes.heading: Heart devices
notes: A defibrillator or other device may be needed for dangerous rhythm or severe pump dysfunction.

heading_notes.heading: Cardiac ablation
notes: Ablation may treat selected rhythm disorders.

heading_notes.heading: Heart transplant
notes: Transplant may be considered for end-stage disease that does not respond to other care.

heading_notes.heading: Labor and delivery
notes: Delivery planning involves cardiology and obstetric specialists and depends on maternal heart status.

heading_notes.heading: Prognosis
notes: Heart function may recover, but persistent impairment and recurrence risk are possible.

heading_notes.heading: Future pregnancies
notes: Future pregnancy may carry substantial risk if heart function has not normalized; specialist counseling is important.

heading_notes.heading: Self-care
notes: Follow medicines, sodium/fluid advice, and activity guidance; monitor symptoms and seek care for worsening breathing or swelling.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring pregnancy/delivery timeline, symptoms, medicines, and family/personal cardiac history.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about heart function, medication safety, breastfeeding, delivery, and future pregnancy risks.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about breathlessness, swelling, pregnancy timing, blood pressure, and cardiac history.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Placenta accreta-Placenta accreta - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Placenta accreta spectrum describes placenta attaching too deeply into the uterine wall, making separation after birth difficult and potentially causing severe hemorrhage.

heading_notes.heading: Placenta accreta
notes: Accreta involves abnormal attachment; deeper invasion into muscle or through the uterine wall is termed increta or percreta.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Often there are no symptoms during pregnancy; vaginal bleeding can occur, especially with associated placenta previa.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Abnormal placental attachment is linked to scarring or changes in the uterine lining.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior cesarean delivery or other uterine surgery, placenta previa, and increasing number of cesareans raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Severe bleeding, transfusion, injury to nearby organs, preterm delivery, hysterectomy, and intensive care may be required.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Ultrasound and sometimes MRI can identify abnormal placental invasion; early diagnosis enables delivery planning at a specialized center.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care generally involves planned cesarean delivery with the placenta left in place and hysterectomy to avoid dangerous separation; timing and approach are individualized.

heading_notes.heading: Before surgery
notes: A multidisciplinary team plans delivery, blood products, anesthesia, and surgical support; emergency risks are discussed.

heading_notes.heading: During surgery
notes: The baby is delivered by cesarean; the placenta is generally not forcibly detached, and hysterectomy may follow to control hemorrhage.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: A high-risk diagnosis and possible hysterectomy can be emotionally difficult; specialist and family support are important.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring imaging, pregnancy history, prior uterine surgeries, and questions about timing, delivery, transfusion, and fertility.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask which specialists will be involved, what symptoms require urgent care, and what recovery/support to expect.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect discussion of placental location, depth, prior cesareans, bleeding risk, delivery timing, and surgical plan.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Placenta previa occurs when the placenta partly or fully covers the cervix; it can cause bleeding and affect delivery planning.

heading_notes.heading: Placenta previa
notes: The placenta lies low in the uterus and reaches or covers the cervical opening.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy is typical; bleeding may stop and recur.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy needs prompt contact with the pregnancy-care team; heavy bleeding is an emergency.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The reason for low placental implantation is not always clear.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior cesarean or uterine surgery, previous placenta previa, multiple pregnancy, older maternal age, and smoking may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Hemorrhage, preterm birth, emergency delivery, and need for cesarean birth are concerns.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Ultrasound identifies placental position; transvaginal imaging may provide a clearer view and is generally safe when performed by clinicians.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on bleeding, gestational age, and placental coverage; monitoring and activity guidance may be used when stable.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment of bleeding
notes: Significant bleeding may require hospital care, fluids or transfusion, and sometimes urgent delivery.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment with no bleeding
notes: If stable, follow-up imaging and monitoring continue; clinicians advise on activity and signs requiring emergency care.

heading_notes.heading: Planned C-section delivery
notes: When the placenta covers the cervix, vaginal delivery is unsafe; cesarean birth is planned, often before labor begins.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Bleeding risk and restrictions can be stressful; discuss practical and emotional support with the care team.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring pregnancy records, bleeding details, prior uterine surgery history, and questions about delivery timing.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about amount/timing of bleeding, contractions, pregnancy dating, and prior cesareans.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: PCOS is a hormonal/metabolic condition involving irregular ovulation, excess androgen effects, and sometimes multiple small ovarian follicles.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Irregular or absent periods, difficulty conceiving, excess facial/body hair, acne, scalp hair thinning, and weight/metabolic changes can occur.

heading_notes.heading: Polycystic ovary
notes: Ultrasound may show many small follicles, but ovarian appearance alone does not establish PCOS.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for persistent irregular periods, trouble conceiving, or signs of androgen excess.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause is not fully known; insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, heredity, and androgen excess are implicated.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Family history, insulin resistance, and excess weight may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Possible effects include infertility, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, sleep apnea, endometrial overgrowth/cancer risk, and pregnancy complications.

notes: Links to related health topics and articles.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Rectocele is posterior vaginal wall prolapse in which the rectum bulges toward the vagina because pelvic support tissue weakens.

heading_notes.heading: Posterior vaginal prolapse (rectocele)
notes: The rectum presses into the back wall of the vagina; stool may collect in the pouch.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Vaginal bulge/pressure, incomplete bowel emptying, constipation, or needing to press on the vagina/perineum to pass stool may occur; mild cases can be symptom-free.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care for a bothersome bulge, bowel-emptying problems, or pain.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Pregnancy and vaginal delivery can stretch or injure pelvic support; aging and chronic pressure also contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Pregnancy and childbirth
notes: Tissue strain, prolonged pushing, and delivery injury may weaken posterior vaginal support.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Vaginal birth, aging, obesity, chronic constipation/cough, heavy lifting, and pelvic surgery can increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Reducing chronic straining, managing constipation/cough, and maintaining pelvic-floor strength may help.

notes: Mild cases may need no treatment; symptoms can be managed with bowel measures, pelvic-floor care, pessary, or surgery.

notes: A vaginal support device may be fitted to support pelvic tissues; regular removal/cleaning and follow-up are needed.

Symptoms & causes.summary: Post-hysterectomy vaginal vault prolapse (PHVP) is the guideline’s condition-specific term for prolapse of the vaginal vault after hysterectomy. Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Pelvic-floor muscle training is effective for stage I–II PHVP, and vaginal pessaries are an alternative for stage II–IV PHVP. Surgery should be offered for symptomatic PHVP after appropriate counseling; abdominal sacrocolpopexy and sacrospinous fixation are both effective primary treatments, with sacrospinous fixation associated with earlier recovery.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Bleeding after menopause may range from light pink, gray, or brown spotting to heavy flow; it is usually painless and should be evaluated promptly. Causes include menopausal thinning of vaginal/vulvar tissue, polyps, and an excessively thick or abnormal uterine lining; cancer is a serious but less common cause.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: ACOG, Bleeding After Menopause Could Be a Problem. Here's What to Know. — Postmenopausal bleeding

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Postpartum preeclampsia is new high blood pressure with signs of organ involvement after childbirth, often within days but sometimes later.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Severe headache, vision changes, upper abdominal pain, nausea, shortness of breath, swelling, or reduced urination may occur; some cases have few signs.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek urgent care for severe headache, vision changes, shortness of breath, chest pain, or severe abdominal pain after delivery.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The exact cause is unknown; pregnancy-related blood-vessel and placental changes may persist after birth.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, obesity, diabetes, kidney disease, autoimmune disease, or multiple pregnancy may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Seizures, stroke, pulmonary edema, organ injury, and blood clots are possible without treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Other high blood pressure disorders during pregnancy

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Preeclampsia is pregnancy-related high blood pressure that can affect organs, often after 20 weeks but sometimes postpartum.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: It may be symptom-free; warning signs include persistent headache, visual disturbance, upper-abdominal pain, nausea, sudden swelling, or shortness of breath.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Report concerning symptoms promptly; severe headache, vision changes, or severe pain require urgent assessment.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The precise cause is unclear; abnormal placental blood-vessel development and maternal vascular responses are implicated.

heading_notes.heading: Other high blood pressure disorders during pregnancy
notes: The page distinguishes chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, and preeclampsia based on timing and organ findings.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior preeclampsia, first pregnancy, multiple gestation, chronic hypertension, kidney disease, diabetes, autoimmune disease, and obesity can raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Other risk factors
notes: Age extremes, long interval between pregnancies, family history, and assisted reproduction may also contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Severe disease can cause seizures, stroke, placental abruption, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and maternal organ injury.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Low-dose aspirin may be recommended for selected high-risk patients; discuss prevention and monitoring with an obstetric clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Medication
notes: Medication and lifestyle choices are discussed in the context of blood-pressure control and pregnancy safety.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and healthy choices
notes: Attend prenatal visits, follow care-team guidance, and manage chronic conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Delivery
notes: Delivery is the definitive treatment; timing balances maternal safety with fetal maturity.

heading_notes.heading: After delivery

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Pregestational diabetes is diabetes present before pregnancy; inadequate insulin production or response leaves glucose in the bloodstream rather than moving it into cells. High glucose early in pregnancy is associated with fetal birth defects, including defects of the heart, brain, spine, and skeleton. Pregnancy with pregestational diabetes is associated with increased risk of high blood pressure and preeclampsia.

Management during pregnancy includes glucose control; medication, diet, and exercise plans may need adjustment. People with diabetes should discuss delivery timing with their obstetric clinician; induction may be considered earlier when pregnancy problems arise.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: NIH/NCBI PMC: Pregnancy After Solid Organ Transplantation: A Guide for Obstetric Management — Pregnancy after transplant
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Successful pregnancies are possible after solid-organ transplantation, but recipients have increased maternal and neonatal complication risks, including prematurity and low birth weight. Hypertension, diabetes, and infection are important pregnancy risks in transplant recipients and require monitoring. Pregnancy is generally advised against for at least one year after transplantation because early pregnancy may adversely affect graft function and fetal well-being.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: NIH/NCBI PMC: Pregnancy After Solid Organ Transplantation: A Guide for Obstetric Management — Pregnancy after transplant
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Care should involve a high-risk obstetrician together with the transplant team and should be multidisciplinary before, during, and after pregnancy. Pregnancy is considered more appropriate when graft function is stable, there has been no rejection in the preceding year, there is no acute infection affecting fetal well-being, and immunosuppression is stable. Immunosuppression is usually maintained at appropriate doses to prevent rejection; mycophenolic acid products should, when possible, be stopped before conception and replaced with an alternative.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Premature birth - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Premature birth is delivery before 37 completed weeks; earlier birth generally increases the chance of medical complications.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Possible labor signs include regular contractions, fluid leakage, bleeding, pelvic pressure, backache, or menstrual-like cramps.

heading_notes.heading: Special care
notes: Premature newborns may need a neonatal intensive care unit for breathing, feeding, temperature, and infection support.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior preterm birth, multiple pregnancy, uterine/cervical conditions, infection, chronic illness, smoking, and short interval between pregnancies may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Risks depend on gestational age and may include breathing, feeding, temperature, infection, vision/hearing, and developmental problems.

heading_notes.heading: Short-term complications
notes: Immature lungs, brain, gut, immune system, and temperature regulation can cause acute newborn illness.

heading_notes.heading: Long-term complications
notes: Some children face chronic lung, vision/hearing, motor, learning, or developmental challenges.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Prenatal care, addressing infections and chronic conditions, avoiding tobacco/drugs, and selected progesterone/cervical interventions may lower risk.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Preterm labor - Symptoms and causes
headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Preterm labor is regular contractions that cause cervical change before 37 weeks; early recognition can allow treatment to improve outcomes.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Signs can include regular uterine tightening, low backache, pelvic pressure, cramps, vaginal discharge change, bleeding, or fluid leakage.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Contact the pregnancy-care team promptly for regular contractions, bleeding, leaking fluid, or significant pressure before 37 weeks.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior preterm birth, multiple gestation, cervical/uterine differences, infection, short cervix, smoking, and pregnancy complications can raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Medical history
notes: Previous preterm labor, pregnancy loss, cervical procedures, or chronic illness affect risk assessment.

heading_notes.heading: Pregnancy issues
notes: Multiple pregnancy, bleeding, infection, short cervix, or placental problems may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Other factors
notes: Smoking, low or high body weight, stress, and short spacing between pregnancies may be associated.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Preterm labor can result in premature birth and related newborn complications.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Prenatal care, smoking cessation, treating infections, and selected progesterone or cervical interventions may reduce risk.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Clinicians assess contraction pattern, cervical change, fetal status, and possible membrane rupture or infection.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care may include short-term delay of delivery, fetal lung-maturation medicine, magnesium for neuroprotection, antibiotics for specific indications, or delivery if needed.

heading_notes.heading: Surgical procedure
notes: A cervical cerclage may be considered for selected patients with cervical insufficiency, typically before labor begins.

heading_notes.heading: Vaginal progesterone
notes: Progesterone may be used in selected pregnancies with a short cervix to reduce preterm birth risk.

heading_notes.heading: Treatments once you're in labor
notes: Tocolytic medicines may briefly slow contractions; corticosteroids and magnesium may be given depending on gestational age and clinical circumstances.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Follow care-team instructions; home measures cannot reliably stop established preterm labor.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Risk and hospitalization can be stressful; seek support and clear communication with the obstetric team.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Know gestational age, contraction timing, fluid/bleeding symptoms, and pregnancy history.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Time contractions and report warning signs promptly.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about contraction frequency, fluid leakage, bleeding, pain, prior preterm birth, and risk factors.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Primary ovarian insufficiency - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Primary ovarian insufficiency occurs when ovarian function declines before age 40, causing irregular periods and reduced estrogen; it is different from typical menopause.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Irregular or missed periods, hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, reduced libido, and difficulty conceiving may occur.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for absent/irregular periods, hot flashes at a young age, or fertility concerns.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Causes include chromosome or gene changes, autoimmune disease, chemotherapy/radiation, surgery, or unknown factors.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Family history, genetic conditions, autoimmune disease, and cancer treatment may raise risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Low estrogen can affect fertility, bone density, cardiovascular health, and emotional wellbeing.

headings: What to expect from your provider

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Repeated hormone testing, pregnancy testing, and evaluation for genetic or autoimmune causes help establish ovarian insufficiency.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Hormone therapy is commonly recommended until the usual age of menopause to replace estrogen and protect bone/overall health unless contraindicated.

heading_notes.heading: Addressing infertility
notes: Spontaneous pregnancy is uncommon but possible; fertility specialists can discuss donor eggs, IVF, or other options.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Weight-bearing exercise, adequate calcium/vitamin D, avoiding smoking, and heart-healthy habits support bone and cardiovascular health.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Infertility and early loss of ovarian function may cause grief; counseling and support groups can help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring menstrual/fertility history, family history, treatments, and questions about hormones and pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about bone-health monitoring, hormone therapy, and reproductive options.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your provider
notes: Expect questions about cycle changes, symptoms, family/genetic history, and cancer treatment.
