headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Bronchopulmonary (pulmonary) sequestration is a congenital lung lesion whose cause is unknown; CHOP reports no established hereditary or chromosomal association. Many affected children have no symptoms. Large lesions can restrict lung growth, shift the heart, impair blood flow, and lead to fetal heart failure with fluid accumulation (hydrops).

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia: Bronchopulmonary Sequestration (BPS) — Pulmonary sequestration
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Most cases are identified on routine ultrasound around 18–20 weeks as a bright solid fetal chest mass; Doppler assessment of lesion blood flow helps distinguish it from other lung lesions. Evaluation may include high-resolution fetal ultrasound, fetal echocardiography, and sometimes fetal MRI; serial ultrasounds monitor lesion growth. Most children can undergo surgery after birth, while rare rapidly growing or life-threatening lesions may require fetal intervention, such as chest-fluid drainage.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Rectovaginal fistula - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: A rectovaginal fistula is an abnormal passage between the rectum and vagina, allowing bowel contents or gas to pass through the vagina.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Possible signs include gas or stool through the vagina, foul discharge, recurrent vaginal/urinary infections, and irritation or pain.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for stool or gas passing through the vagina, unusual discharge, or recurrent infection.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Fistulas may follow difficult childbirth injury, pelvic surgery, Crohn disease or other bowel inflammation, cancer, radiation, or infection.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Obstructed/prolonged labor, pelvic procedures, inflammatory bowel disease, cancer treatment, and tissue infection can increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Infection, skin irritation, pain, and emotional/social distress may occur.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Prompt management of childbirth injury, infection, and bowel disease may reduce some risks; not all causes are preventable.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation includes medical/obstetric history and physical examination; dye, endoscopy, or imaging may locate the tract and identify underlying disease.

heading_notes.heading: Physical exam
notes: Inspection and pelvic/rectal examination can reveal an opening, inflammation, or related tissue injury.

heading_notes.heading: Tests for identifying fistulas
notes: Dye tests, endoscopy, MRI, or other imaging may map the fistula and assess bowel/vaginal structures.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Small or inflamed fistulas may be managed first with infection/inflammation treatment and local care; persistent fistulas often need surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Antibiotics or treatment for Crohn disease/other underlying inflammation may be used when indicated.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Repair may close the tract and restore tissue separation; timing and technique depend on cause, size, infection, and tissue health.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Keep the area clean and dry and follow bowel-care instructions to reduce irritation.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring childbirth, bowel-disease, surgery, radiation, and infection history plus symptom details.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about repair timing, recurrence, bowel management, and expected recovery.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about leakage, childbirth injuries, bowel symptoms, prior surgery, and inflammatory disease.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG): Repeated Miscarriages — Recurrent miscarriage
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: ACOG defines recurrent pregnancy loss as two or more miscarriages and recommends physical examination and testing after two losses. About half of miscarriages occur randomly when an embryo has an abnormal chromosome number; the chance increases with age. Potential contributors to repeated loss include a parental chromosomal translocation, a uterine septum or scarring (Asherman syndrome), and antiphospholipid syndrome.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: NHS — Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) — Rh disease
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Can occur when a D-negative pregnant person carries a D-positive baby and develops antibodies that break down the baby's red blood cells. After birth, the baby is monitored for jaundice and anaemia.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features

After birth, the baby is monitored for jaundice and anaemia.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: NHS — Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) — Rh disease
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Pregnancy screening includes a blood test at the first antenatal appointment; if the pregnant person is D-negative and the baby is D-positive, an additional risk assessment is performed. Management may include injections to prevent antibody formation, fetal blood transfusion and weekly immunoglobulin treatment; affected newborns may receive phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: American Society for Reproductive Medicine — Evidence-based diagnosis and treatment for uterine septum: a guideline — Septate uterus
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: A uterine septum occurs when tissue connecting the two paramesonephric ducts fails to resorb before the 20th embryonic week. Septate uteri are often asymptomatic; the condition is associated with spontaneous abortion and obstetric complications.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: American Society for Reproductive Medicine — Evidence-based diagnosis and treatment for uterine septum: a guideline — Septate uterus
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: ASRM recommends 3D transvaginal ultrasound, with or without saline infusion, as the first-line noninvasive diagnostic tool. Hysteroscopic septum incision is recommended as a shared-decision option for patients with a septum and recurrent miscarriage; in infertility, incision may be offered after counseling because live-birth benefit remains uncertain.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Sexually transmitted infections spread mainly through sexual contact; many cause no symptoms but can affect reproductive health and newborns.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Possible signs vary by infection and include genital sores or bumps, unusual discharge, painful urination, pelvic pain, bleeding, rash, or no symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek testing after possible exposure, with symptoms, or before/with a new partner; some infections need prompt treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Unprotected sex, multiple/new partners, prior STI, and substance use affecting safer-sex decisions increase exposure risk.

heading_notes.heading: Spread from mothers to infants
notes: Some infections can pass during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding and cause serious newborn illness.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Untreated infection may lead to infertility, pelvic inflammatory disease, pregnancy complications, cancers, organ/neurologic disease, or increased HIV transmission risk.

notes: Vaccination where available, condoms/barriers, testing, mutually agreed safer-sex practices, and prompt treatment reduce risk.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Small bowel prolapse (enterocele) - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Enterocele is small-bowel prolapse into the upper vagina when pelvic support weakens.

heading_notes.heading: Small bowel prolapse (enterocele)
notes: The small intestine descends and pushes against the vaginal wall; it may occur with other pelvic-organ prolapse.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Pelvic pressure or fullness, a vaginal bulge, low-back discomfort, or symptoms that worsen with standing/straining may occur; some cases are silent.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek assessment for a vaginal bulge, pelvic pressure, or bowel/bladder changes.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Pelvic support can weaken after pregnancy and childbirth, hysterectomy, aging, or chronic pressure.

heading_notes.heading: Pregnancy and childbirth
notes: Pregnancy and vaginal delivery stretch supporting tissues and can contribute to prolapse.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, childbirth, obesity, chronic cough/constipation, heavy lifting, and pelvic surgery may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Avoiding chronic straining, managing weight/cough/constipation, and pelvic-floor strengthening may help.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Spina bifida is a neural-tube defect in which the spine and spinal cord do not develop or close completely during early pregnancy.

heading_notes.heading: Types
notes: Forms range from occult spina bifida with few signs to meningocele and myelomeningocele, which can involve exposed nerves and significant disability.

heading_notes.heading: Spina bifida (myelomeningocele)
notes: Myelomeningocele is the most severe common form; spinal cord and nerves protrude through an opening and may be damaged.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Effects vary by type and may include weakness/paralysis, sensory loss, bladder/bowel dysfunction, hydrocephalus, and orthopedic problems.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Prenatal screening findings should be discussed with maternal-fetal specialists; newborn symptoms require prompt pediatric evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The exact cause is unclear; genetic, nutritional, and environmental factors may interact during early neural-tube formation.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Folate deficiency, certain antiseizure medicines, diabetes, obesity, elevated body temperature early in pregnancy, and family history can increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Possible issues include mobility limitations, hydrocephalus, Chiari II malformation, latex allergy, skin problems, and bladder/bowel dysfunction.

heading_notes.heading: Other complications
notes: Additional orthopedic, neurologic, learning, and psychosocial needs may require lifelong multidisciplinary care.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy reduces neural-tube-defect risk.

heading_notes.heading: Get folic acid first
notes: Begin recommended folic acid before pregnancy because neural-tube closure occurs very early.

heading_notes.heading: Planning pregnancy
notes: People with prior affected pregnancy or risk factors should discuss supplementation and medication safety before conception.

heading_notes.heading: When higher doses are needed
notes: Clinicians may recommend higher-dose folic acid for selected high-risk patients; use clinician guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Prenatal screening may use maternal blood tests, ultrasound, and amniocentesis; postnatal examination and imaging assess spinal and brain effects.

heading_notes.heading: Blood tests
notes: Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein screening can indicate increased risk and prompt further evaluation.

heading_notes.heading: Ultrasound
notes: Detailed fetal ultrasound can identify spinal opening and related brain changes.

heading_notes.heading: Amniocentesis
notes: Amniotic-fluid testing may help confirm a fetal neural-tube defect after counseling.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on type and severity and may include fetal or postnatal surgery plus ongoing neurologic, orthopedic, bladder, and bowel management.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery before birth
notes: Fetal repair may be considered in selected cases at specialized centers, balancing potential neurologic benefit against maternal and pregnancy risks.

heading_notes.heading: Cesarean birth
notes: Delivery planning may favor cesarean birth after fetal repair or based on fetal/spinal considerations.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery after birth
notes: Newborn repair closes the spinal opening and protects exposed tissue; it does not reverse existing nerve injury.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment for complications
notes: Hydrocephalus, mobility, orthopedic issues, and bladder/bowel dysfunction may require additional procedures and therapies.

heading_notes.heading: Ongoing care
notes: Multidisciplinary follow-up supports mobility, learning, skin health, continence, and transition to adult care.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Families may benefit from counseling, peer support, and coordinated specialty care.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring prenatal screening results, family/genetic history, and questions about fetal surgery, delivery, and long-term care.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask about folic acid for future pregnancies and developmental/medical follow-up.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect discussion of defect location, fetal brain findings, mobility prognosis, and treatment risks.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Stress incontinence - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Stress incontinence is urine leakage during physical pressure, such as coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting, or exercise.

heading_notes.heading: Female urinary system
notes: The kidneys produce urine, which travels via ureters to the bladder and exits through the urethra.

heading_notes.heading: Male urinary system
notes: Male urinary anatomy includes the bladder and urethra, with the prostate affecting outlet function.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Leakage occurs with exertion or pressure, usually without the urgency typical of overactive bladder.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation when leakage affects daily activity or quality of life.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Weak pelvic-floor or urethral support prevents closure when abdominal pressure rises.

heading_notes.heading: Female pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic muscles support bladder/urethra and help maintain continence.

heading_notes.heading: Male pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic-floor and sphincter support contribute to urinary control.

heading_notes.heading: Female stress incontinence
notes: Pregnancy, vaginal birth, menopause-related changes, obesity, and pelvic procedures may weaken support.

heading_notes.heading: Male stress incontinence
notes: Prostate surgery or pelvic treatment can weaken urinary sphincter function.

heading_notes.heading: Other factors
notes: Chronic cough, constipation, smoking, and heavy lifting can increase abdominal pressure.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Childbirth, aging, obesity, pelvic surgery, and chronic pressure are associated risks.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Leakage can cause skin irritation, embarrassment, and limits on work, exercise, and social activity.

headings: What to expect from your healthcare professional

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: History, physical/pelvic examination, urine testing, and bladder-function tests identify leakage type and contributing factors.

heading_notes.heading: Tests of bladder function
notes: Urine tests, post-void residual measurement, stress testing, and urodynamic studies may clarify bladder and sphincter function.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Pelvic-floor training and behavioral care are common first steps; devices, medicines, or surgery may be considered based on sex and severity.

heading_notes.heading: Behavior therapies
notes: Bladder habits, weight management, fluid timing, and pelvic-floor exercise can reduce leakage.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Some medicines may improve urethral closure or support, depending on local approval and patient factors.

heading_notes.heading: Female stress incontinence
notes: Options may include pelvic-floor therapy, vaginal support devices, urethral bulking, or sling surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Devices
notes: Pessaries or urethral inserts can support the urethra for selected patients.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Sling procedures and other operations support the urethra; choice depends on anatomy, prior surgery, and goals.

heading_notes.heading: Male stress incontinence
notes: Male slings or artificial urinary sphincters may be considered, often after prostate treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Clinical trials
notes: Research studies may offer investigational approaches.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Pelvic-floor exercises, weight management, reducing bladder irritants, and smoking cessation may help.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Planning for leakage and discussing sexual/social concerns can support quality of life.

heading_notes.heading: Going out and about
notes: Planning toilet access and carrying supplies may reduce anxiety outside the home.

heading_notes.heading: Sex and incontinence
notes: Leakage during sex can be discussed with clinicians; emptying the bladder and practical measures may help.

heading_notes.heading: Seek help
notes: Professional evaluation can identify options even when symptoms feel embarrassing.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring leakage triggers, frequency, prior pelvic/prostate surgery, medicines, and questions.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track leakage and fluid intake and ask which treatments fit the cause.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your healthcare professional
notes: Expect questions about triggers, childbirth/prostate history, urinary symptoms, and impact.

Symptoms & causes.summary: Thoracic endometriosis syndrome can manifest as catamenial pneumothorax, hemothorax, hemoptysis, or pulmonary nodules. Symptoms commonly occur in temporal association with menstruation; pleuritic chest pain, cough, and shortness of breath are described. Thoracic disease is often associated with pelvic endometriosis and is predominantly right-sided.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: TAPS occurs in monochorionic twin pregnancies when small placental arteriovenous connections cause chronic, unidirectional transfusion from an anemic donor twin to a polycythemic recipient twin. Unlike twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, TAPS does not feature the oligohydramnios–polyhydramnios sequence.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Prenatal diagnosis uses Doppler ultrasound of middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity; a delta value greater than 0.5 multiples of the median is a diagnostic criterion in the reviewed source. Management is individualized and may include expectant ultrasound/Doppler monitoring, intrauterine transfusion, or fetoscopic laser treatment.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: National Library of Medicine (PMC): Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence: Prenatal Diagnosis and Treatment — Twin reversed arterial perfusion (TRAP) sequence
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: A rare complication of monochorionic multiple pregnancy in which an acardiac twin is perfused by a structurally normal pump twin through placental vascular connections. The pump twin is at risk of hyperdynamic circulation and high-output cardiac failure; concerning findings include hydrops, cardiomegaly, polyhydramnios, or continued growth of the acardiac twin.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: National Library of Medicine (PMC): Twin Reversed Arterial Perfusion Sequence: Prenatal Diagnosis and Treatment — Twin reversed arterial perfusion (TRAP) sequence
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Ultrasound with color Doppler identifies reversed blood flow into the abnormal twin through its umbilical artery; ultrasound and Doppler are used to monitor the pump twin. Management may include close surveillance; when treatment is indicated, ultrasound-guided laser coagulation or radiofrequency ablation interrupts blood supply to the acardiac twin.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) Consult Series #72 — Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: TTTS is associated with a shared placental circulation in monochorionic twin gestations. Ultrasound surveillance assesses amniotic-fluid volume on both sides of the intertwin membrane and whether each fetal bladder is urine-filled; umbilical-artery Doppler assessment is also recommended.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) Consult Series #72 — Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome (TTTS)
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: SMFM recommends beginning TTTS ultrasound surveillance at 16 weeks in monochorionic-diamniotic pregnancies and repeating it at least every 2 weeks. Fetoscopic laser surgery is the standard treatment for stage II through stage IV TTTS presenting at 16–26 weeks; asymptomatic stage I cases generally receive at least weekly surveillance.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Cleveland Clinic: Urethral Diverticulum (UD): Symptoms, Treatments & Tests — Urethral diverticulum
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: A urethral diverticulum is a pocket or sac that forms along the urethra; it can fill with urine or pus and lead to infection. Symptoms may include recurrent urinary tract infections, post-void urine dribbling, dysuria, urinary urgency, hematuria, or pain with intercourse; some patients have no symptoms.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation can include pelvic examination, MRI, ultrasound, and cystoscopy to identify the diverticulum and its opening. Surgery is often the preferred treatment; options include removal of the sac, opening its neck to drain it, or creating a drainage opening, with follow-up monitoring for those who defer surgery.

headings: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, has been recognized as one of the top Urology hospitals in the nation by U.S. News & World Report.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Urinary incontinence is involuntary urine leakage; types include stress, urge, overflow, functional, and mixed patterns.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Symptoms depend on type: leakage with exertion, sudden urgency, frequent dribbling/incomplete emptying, or difficulty reaching a toilet.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care when leakage is frequent, bothersome, or associated with blood, pain, or difficulty urinating.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Temporary causes include infection, constipation, or medicines; persistent causes include pelvic-floor weakness, neurologic disease, obstruction, and bladder overactivity.

heading_notes.heading: Female urinary system
notes: Kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra form the urinary tract.

heading_notes.heading: Male urinary system
notes: The male urinary tract includes kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra, and prostate.

heading_notes.heading: Temporary urinary incontinence
notes: Infection, foods/drinks, alcohol/caffeine, constipation, or short-term medicines may trigger reversible leakage.

heading_notes.heading: Persistent urinary incontinence
notes: Ongoing leakage may arise from muscle weakness, nerve damage, prostate enlargement, obstruction, or chronic bladder conditions.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Age, obesity, smoking, diabetes, neurologic disease, pregnancy/childbirth, and pelvic surgery increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Skin problems, urinary infection, sleep disruption, and social/emotional effects may occur.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Healthy weight, pelvic-floor exercise, limiting bladder irritants, and avoiding constipation may reduce risk.

What to expect from your doctor
Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, has been recognized as one of the top Urology hospitals in the nation by U.S. News & World Report.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation includes history, exam, urine testing, post-void residual measurement, and selected bladder-function studies.

heading_notes.heading: Care at Mayo Clinic
notes: Link to Mayo Clinic care and appointment resources.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Treatment depends on leakage type and cause and ranges from behavior and pelvic-floor therapy to medicines, devices, procedures, or surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Behavioral techniques
notes: Bladder training, scheduled voiding, double voiding, and fluid adjustments can improve control.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic floor muscle exercises
notes: Kegel exercises strengthen muscles supporting urinary control.

heading_notes.heading: Female pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic-floor anatomy supports bladder and urethra.

heading_notes.heading: Male pelvic floor muscles
notes: Pelvic muscles and sphincter contribute to continence.

heading_notes.heading: Medications
notes: Drugs may relax bladder, reduce urgency, or address prostate-related obstruction depending on cause.

heading_notes.heading: Electrical stimulation
notes: Stimulation can strengthen pelvic-floor response or modify bladder signals.

heading_notes.heading: Medical devices
notes: Devices may support the urethra or assist emptying.

heading_notes.heading: Types of pessaries
notes: Vaginal pessaries can support pelvic organs and reduce stress leakage in selected women.

heading_notes.heading: Interventional therapies
notes: Bulking agents and nerve-stimulation approaches may be options when conservative care is insufficient.

heading_notes.heading: Sacral nerve stimulator
notes: An implanted device modulates nerve signals for selected urgency/incontinence cases.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Procedures can support the bladder/urethra or address obstruction, selected by leakage type.

heading_notes.heading: Bladder neck suspension
notes: A procedure lifts/supports the bladder neck to reduce stress leakage.

heading_notes.heading: Absorbent pads and catheters
notes: Containment products and intermittent catheters can manage symptoms when other strategies are insufficient.

heading_notes.heading: From Mayo Clinic to your inbox
notes: Newsletter subscription information.

heading_notes.heading: Clinical trials
notes: Research options may be available.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Weight management, fluid/caffeine adjustment, timed voiding, and constipation care can help.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence is limited; discuss complementary treatments and supplements.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Support and practical planning can reduce effects on daily life.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring bladder diary, symptoms, medicines, prior surgeries, and questions.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track episodes and triggers and ask about treatment choices.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about leakage type, frequency, triggers, urinary history, and impact.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: An isthmocele is a pouch or scar-tissue defect in the front uterine wall that can form when a prior cesarean incision does not heal completely. Symptoms may include irregular or intermenstrual bleeding, painful periods, pain during sex, and pelvic pain; some people have no symptoms.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Uterine polyps-Uterine polyps - Symptoms & causes - Mayo Clinic

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Uterine polyps are growths attached to the endometrium; most are benign, though some may be precancerous or cancerous.

heading_notes.heading: Uterine polyps
notes: Polyps may be small or large and may protrude into the uterine cavity.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Irregular bleeding, bleeding between periods or after menopause, unusually heavy periods, and infertility may occur; some polyps are asymptomatic.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for persistent irregular/heavy bleeding or any postmenopausal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Growth is linked to estrogen stimulation of the uterine lining.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Perimenopause/postmenopause, obesity, hypertension, and tamoxifen use may increase likelihood.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Most polyps are benign; some contain abnormal cells, and they may contribute to fertility problems.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Evaluation may include transvaginal ultrasound, saline sonohysterography, hysteroscopy, and tissue sampling.

heading_notes.heading: Transvaginal ultrasound
notes: A vaginal probe images the uterine cavity and lining.

heading_notes.heading: Hysterosonography
notes: Fluid expands the cavity during ultrasound to outline polyps more clearly.

heading_notes.heading: Hysteroscopy
notes: A lighted scope allows direct inspection and sometimes removal of a polyp.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Observation may be reasonable for small symptom-free polyps; symptomatic, persistent, or concerning lesions may be removed and examined.

heading_notes.heading: More Information

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring bleeding history, medicines, pregnancy goals, and questions about removal and pathology.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Record cycle/bleeding changes and ask whether follow-up or tissue testing is needed.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about periods, pregnancy, tamoxifen, and abnormal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Uterine prolapse occurs when weakened pelvic support allows the uterus to descend into or protrude through the vagina.

heading_notes.heading: Uterine prolapse
notes: Severity ranges from slight descent to the uterus extending outside the vaginal opening.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Uterine sarcoma - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Uterine sarcoma is a rare cancer that begins in uterine muscle or supporting tissue; it differs from the more common endometrial cancer.

heading_notes.heading: Types
notes: Types include leiomyosarcoma, endometrial stromal sarcoma, and other uncommon uterine sarcomas.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain/pressure, or a growing pelvic mass may occur.

heading_notes.heading: When to seek care
notes: Seek prompt evaluation for postmenopausal bleeding or persistent unusual bleeding, pain, or pelvic fullness.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The exact cause is unknown; cancer develops after cell changes drive uncontrolled growth.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior pelvic radiation and some hormone or genetic factors may be associated; many cases have no clear risk factor.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Imaging and tissue sampling help determine tumor location, type, and grade; diagnosis may require specialist pathology.

heading_notes.heading: Imaging tests
notes: Ultrasound, MRI, CT, or other scans assess uterine mass and possible spread.

heading_notes.heading: Tissue testing
notes: Biopsy or surgical tissue examination identifies tumor type; some sarcomas are difficult to distinguish from benign fibroids before surgery.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Grades
notes: Grade describes how abnormal/aggressive tumor cells look and helps estimate behavior.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care depends on sarcoma subtype, grade, spread, health, and fertility goals; surgery is common, with other therapies selected as needed.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery
notes: Hysterectomy is often used; removal of ovaries/tubes and staging procedures depend on tumor type and spread.

heading_notes.heading: Chemotherapy
notes: Systemic medicines may be used for advanced, recurrent, or higher-risk disease.

heading_notes.heading: Hormone therapy
notes: Hormone-blocking medicines may help selected hormone-sensitive sarcomas.

heading_notes.heading: Radiation therapy
notes: Radiation may reduce local recurrence risk or treat disease not fully removed.

heading_notes.heading: Targeted therapy and immunotherapy
notes: These may be options for selected advanced tumors based on tumor features.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Cancer care, fertility concerns, and uncertainty can be emotionally demanding; support services and trusted relationships help.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring imaging/pathology records, symptoms, medicines, and questions about tumor subtype, stage, fertility, and treatment.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask whether specialist pathology review or clinical trials are appropriate.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about bleeding, pelvic symptoms, menopause, prior radiation, and family history.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Vaginal agenesis is a congenital condition in which the vagina is absent or underdeveloped; uterine and urinary anatomy may also differ.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: A person may not menstruate by expected puberty age, have monthly pelvic pain if menstrual flow is obstructed, or notice difficulty with intercourse.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Evaluation is appropriate when menstruation has not begun by expected age or there is cyclic pelvic pain or vaginal anatomy concern.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The reproductive tract does not form typically during fetal development; the exact cause is often unclear.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Fertility and sexual function depend on uterine and vaginal anatomy; obstructed menstrual flow can cause pain or infection.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Vaginal atrophy, also called genitourinary syndrome of menopause, reflects thinning/drying/inflammation of vaginal and urinary tissues as estrogen falls.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Vaginal dryness, burning, irritation, pain with sex, urinary urgency/frequency, painful urination, and recurrent urinary infections may occur.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care for persistent vaginal/urinary symptoms or bleeding, especially after menopause.

heading_notes.heading: Vaginal dryness
notes: Low estrogen reduces moisture and elasticity, which can make sex painful and tissues fragile.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Menopause is common; breastfeeding, ovarian removal, cancer therapies, and medicines that lower estrogen can also contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Smoking, low estrogen states, sexual inactivity, and cancer treatments that affect estrogen may increase symptoms.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Painful intercourse, recurrent urinary infections, and urinary symptoms can affect quality of life.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Regular sexual activity may promote blood flow; moisturizers and early care can reduce discomfort.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

headings: What to expect from your doctor

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Medical history and pelvic examination assess tissue changes; testing may rule out infection or other causes.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic exam
notes: Examination checks vaginal tissue for thinning, dryness, inflammation, or other abnormalities.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Nonhormonal and hormonal options are chosen by symptom severity, health history, and cancer risk.

heading_notes.heading: Vaginal moisturizers or lubricants
notes: Moisturizers used regularly and lubricants during sex can reduce dryness and friction.

heading_notes.heading: Topical estrogen
notes: Low-dose vaginal estrogen can improve local symptoms with limited systemic exposure; formulation and safety need clinician review.

heading_notes.heading: Ospemifene (Osphena)
notes: An oral selective estrogen receptor modulator can treat painful intercourse/dryness in selected patients.

heading_notes.heading: Prasterone (Intrarosa)
notes: A vaginal DHEA insert may improve painful sex associated with tissue changes.

heading_notes.heading: Systemic estrogen therapy
notes: Systemic hormone therapy may help broader menopausal symptoms but has different risks; individualize use.

heading_notes.heading: Vaginal dilators
notes: Dilators can gradually improve vaginal flexibility and comfort.

heading_notes.heading: Topical lidocaine
notes: Local anesthetic may reduce pain for selected patients.

heading_notes.heading: If you've had breast cancer
notes: Discuss all hormone-related treatments with the oncology team; nonhormonal care is often tried first.

heading_notes.heading: Self care
notes: Use gentle unscented products, moisturizers, and lubricant; avoid irritants.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence and safety of supplements vary; discuss use with a clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring symptom and cancer/menopause history, medicines, and questions about hormone safety.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Ask which treatment is local versus systemic and what follow-up is appropriate.

heading_notes.heading: What to expect from your doctor
notes: Expect questions about symptoms, sexual activity, menopause, urinary infections, and cancer history.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Vaginal bleeding
headings: Noncancerous growths and other uterine conditions

heading_notes.heading: Definition
notes: Vaginal bleeding outside expected menstruation or after menopause may arise from reproductive, hormonal, infectious, medication-related, or traumatic causes.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Possible causes span pregnancy-related events, cervical/uterine disease, hormone changes, infections, medicines/devices, benign growths, and injury.

heading_notes.heading: Cancers and precancerous conditions
notes: Cervical, uterine, vaginal, or vulvar precancer/cancer can cause abnormal bleeding, especially after menopause or after sex.

heading_notes.heading: Endocrine system factors
notes: Hormone imbalance, thyroid disease, or ovulatory changes may alter bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Fertility and reproduction factors
notes: Pregnancy, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, postpartum changes, and fertility treatments can cause bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Infections
notes: Cervicitis, vaginitis, and sexually transmitted infections may cause spotting or bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Medical conditions
notes: Bleeding disorders and systemic disease can affect menstrual flow.

heading_notes.heading: Medications and devices
notes: Hormonal contraception, IUDs, anticoagulants, and some medicines may change bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Noncancerous growths and other uterine conditions
notes: Fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, and endometrial changes are possible sources.

heading_notes.heading: Trauma
notes: Injury or sexual trauma can cause vaginal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek urgent care for heavy bleeding, faintness, severe pain, pregnancy-associated bleeding, or postmenopausal bleeding.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause is unknown; cell DNA changes drive abnormal growth.

heading_notes.heading: Layers of vaginal tissue
notes: Vaginal wall layers contain different cell types from which distinct tumor types can develop.

heading_notes.heading: Types of vaginal cancer
notes: Squamous cell carcinoma is most common; adenocarcinoma and other rare types also occur.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Older age and persistent high-risk HPV are important risks; smoking and prior exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) before birth are additional risks.

heading_notes.heading: Increasing age
notes: Vaginal cancer is more common in older adults.

heading_notes.heading: Exposure to human papillomavirus
notes: Persistent oncogenic HPV infection raises risk.

heading_notes.heading: Smoking
notes: Tobacco exposure is associated with increased risk.

heading_notes.heading: Exposure to miscarriage prevention medicine
notes: In-utero DES exposure is linked to a rare vaginal cancer subtype.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Tumor growth can affect nearby pelvic organs and may spread to lymph nodes or distant sites.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: HPV vaccination and recommended cervical/pelvic screening may reduce risk or support early detection.

heading_notes.heading: Seek out regular pelvic exams and Pap tests
notes: Follow screening guidance; Pap testing may detect some vaginal/cervical abnormalities.

heading_notes.heading: Consider the HPV vaccine

heading_notes.heading: Surgery

diagnostics.diagnostic_use: Educational, condition-oriented findings. Findings support a differential diagnosis; they do not establish a diagnosis in isolation or replace local protocols.
diagnostics.result_interpretation: “Low/early”, “intermediate”, and “high/advanced” describe a possible increasing burden or concern, not universal laboratory reference ranges.

findings: Mammography is for breast symptoms/screening and is not a staging test for most non-breast gynecologic malignancies.

tests.specimen_or_method: Diagnostic breast imaging protocol
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: focal asymmetry or suspicious calcifications assigned a BI-RADS assessment and recommended next step.
tests.interpretation: Use only for breast indication; imaging assessment does not replace tissue diagnosis.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no suspicious mammographic correlate.

radiology/mammography.child_schema: Each test is an educational example; result wording is illustrative, not a fixed diagnostic criterion or an order recommendation.

findings: Transvaginal/pelvic ultrasound assesses lesion size, location, cystic/solid composition, septations, papillary projections, vascularity, endometrial thickness, myometrial pattern, and free fluid.
pertinent_negatives: Simple thin-walled cyst without solid vascular components is a reassuring descriptor; a normal scan does not exclude microscopic disease.

severity_or_range.low_or_early: Small simple/benign-appearing or subtle focal finding.
severity_or_range.intermediate: Persistent, enlarging, complex, or indeterminate lesion.
severity_or_range.high_or_advanced: Solid/vascular components, papillary projections, ascites, invasion, metastasis, or rapidly enlarging suspicious mass.

tests.specimen_or_method: High-frequency transvaginal pelvic imaging with Doppler when indicated
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: 4.8-cm complex adnexal lesion with solid vascular mural nodule and free pelvic fluid; alternatively, focal endometrial polyp/fibroid/adenomyosis features described with dimensions.
tests.interpretation: Complexity, vascularity, and associated fluid increase concern and guide specialist work-up; morphology is not histology.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no adnexal mass, no free fluid, and no focal endometrial lesion visualized within technical limits.

ultrasound/transvaginal.child_schema: Each test is an educational example; result wording is illustrative, not a fixed diagnostic criterion or an order recommendation.

findings: MRI better characterizes myometrial, endometrial, adnexal, soft-tissue, and local invasion features when ultrasound is indeterminate.
pertinent_negatives: No restricted diffusion/invasion is supportive but not definitive for benignity.

tests.specimen_or_method: Multiplanar soft-tissue MRI; contrast only when appropriate to context
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: T2-hypointense junctional-zone thickening with myometrial cysts (adenomyosis pattern), deep infiltrating endometriosis, indeterminate adnexal lesion, or local tumor extension characterized.
tests.interpretation: Problem-solving/staging modality after or alongside ultrasound; report must describe location, size, invasion, and involved structures.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no definite deep invasion, complex fistula tract, or extra-organ extension identified.

mri.child_schema: Each test is an educational example; result wording is illustrative, not a fixed diagnostic criterion or an order recommendation.

findings: CT is commonly used for suspected extra-pelvic spread, nodal/peritoneal disease, acute complication, or surgical planning; it is not the usual first test for a small benign-appearing pelvic lesion.
pertinent_negatives: No metastatic disease on CT does not exclude microscopic spread.

tests.specimen_or_method: Cross-sectional CT with protocol/contrast selected for indication
tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: complex pelvic mass with omental nodularity/ascites, abscess, hydronephrosis, or alternative acute abdominal process; size and distribution explicitly stated.
tests.interpretation: Useful for acute differential, complication, or malignancy staging—not routine first-line imaging for most benign gynecologic symptoms.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no bowel obstruction, drainable abscess, hydronephrosis, or CT evidence of distant metastasis.

findings: Endometrial biopsy may show hyperplasia, atypia, carcinoma, or benign cycling endometrium; image-guided/surgical tissue establishes many suspected malignancies. Tumor markers alone do not diagnose cancer.
pertinent_negatives: Benign/negative sampling can be falsely reassuring if inadequate or discordant with persistent symptoms/imaging.

tests.test_name: Cervical cytology with high-risk HPV testing
tests.specimen_or_method: Liquid-based cervical sample / validated HPV assay
tests.example_indicative_result: Example: HSIL cytology with high-risk HPV detected; colposcopy-directed biopsy subsequently shows CIN 2/3.
tests.interpretation: Abnormal screening indicates risk and directs colposcopy; cytology/HPV does not alone equal invasive cancer.
tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: NILM cytology with negative high-risk HPV on an adequate sample lowers near-term risk.

pertinent_negatives: No palpable mass does not exclude small, deep, or early disease.

tests.specimen_or_method: Consent-based examination; chaperone/trauma-informed approach as appropriate
tests.example_indicative_result: Example: cervical-motion/adnexal tenderness; enlarged irregular uterus; friable bleeding cervical lesion; prolapse on Valsalva; mucopurulent discharge; or closed/open cervical os documented.

notes: A vaginal fistula is an abnormal connection between the vagina and bladder, urethra, bowel, or another nearby organ.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for unexplained vaginal leakage, recurrent infection, or persistent discharge.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Childbirth injury, pelvic surgery, cancer, radiation, inflammatory bowel disease, infection, or trauma may create a fistula.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Difficult labor, pelvic procedures, cancer/radiation, Crohn disease, and tissue infection may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Repeated infections, skin irritation, social distress, and kidney or bowel problems may occur.

notes: Prompt care for childbirth injury, infection, and bowel disease may lower some risks.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Vaginitis is inflammation of the vagina that may cause discharge, itching, irritation, or pain; cause-specific treatment is important.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Changes in discharge, odor, itching, burning, painful urination, or painful sex may occur; symptoms vary by cause.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek care for first-time symptoms, fever/pelvic pain, pregnancy, recurrent symptoms, or possible STI exposure.

heading_notes.heading: Wait-and-see approach
notes: Avoid self-diagnosis when symptoms are new or recurrent; examination may be needed to distinguish infection from irritation.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Causes include bacterial imbalance, yeast overgrowth, trichomoniasis, low-estrogen tissue changes, and chemical/allergic irritation.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Antibiotics, hormonal changes, diabetes, immune suppression, douching, and sexual exposures may contribute depending on type.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Untreated infection can lead to pelvic infection or pregnancy complications; irritation can persist when the cause is not addressed.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Avoid douching and scented irritants, use safer-sex practices, and manage diabetes or other contributing conditions.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: The typical symptom is continuous urinary leakage through the vagina; a small fistula may instead cause watery vaginal discharge while normal urination continues. Causes include obstructed labor, pelvic surgery (especially hysterectomy), radiation, malignancy, and uncommon congenital or inflammatory causes.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Vesicovaginal Fistula: Diagnosis and Management (NIH/NCBI PMC) — Vesicovaginal fistula
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis can be confirmed with bladder filling and a methylene-blue dye/tampon test; cystoscopy helps locate the tract, and imaging can further define anatomy. Small, early fistulas may close with prolonged catheter drainage, but most require surgical repair; timing and vaginal versus abdominal approach depend on tissue condition and fistula complexity.

tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no adnexal mass, no free fluid, and no focal endometrial lesion visualized within technical limits.

pertinent_negatives: No restricted diffusion/invasion is supportive but not definitive for benignity.

tests.example_indicative_result: Example report: T2-hypointense junctional-zone thickening with myometrial cysts (adenomyosis pattern), deep infiltrating endometriosis, indeterminate adnexal lesion, or local tumor extension characterized.

tests.pertinent_negative_example: Example negative: no definite deep invasion, complex fistula tract, or extra-organ extension identified.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Vulvodynia - Symptoms and causes

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Vulvodynia is chronic vulvar pain lasting at least three months without an identifiable cause; pain can affect sexual activity and daily function.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Burning, stinging, rawness, irritation, or pain may be generalized or localized and triggered by touch, sex, tampon insertion, sitting, or spontaneous.

heading_notes.heading: Vulva
notes: The vulva includes external genital structures surrounding the vaginal opening.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for persistent vulvar pain or discomfort.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: The cause is unclear; nerve injury, inflammation, hormonal factors, pelvic-floor dysfunction, prior infection, or genetic susceptibility may contribute.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Prior recurrent infections, skin conditions, pelvic-floor problems, or nerve sensitivity may be associated.

heading_notes.heading: Complications
notes: Chronic pain can affect sexual function, relationships, sleep, mood, and quality of life.

heading_notes.heading: Diagnosis
notes: Diagnosis is made after examination and tests exclude infection, skin disease, or other identifiable causes.

heading_notes.heading: Pelvic exam
notes: Cotton-swab mapping may locate sensitive areas; pelvic-floor and skin examination assess contributors.

heading_notes.heading: More Information
notes: Supplementary links to tests, procedures, or additional information.

heading_notes.heading: Treatment
notes: Care is individualized and may combine pain medicines, pelvic-floor therapy, topical treatments, counseling, and rarely surgery.

heading_notes.heading: Medicines
notes: Topical anesthetics, nerve-pain medicines, or selected antidepressants/anticonvulsants may reduce pain.

heading_notes.heading: Therapies
notes: Pelvic-floor physical therapy, biofeedback, and counseling/sex therapy can address muscle and emotional effects.

heading_notes.heading: Surgery or other procedures
notes: Vestibulectomy may help selected localized provoked vestibular pain after other treatments fail.

heading_notes.heading: Alternative medicine
notes: Evidence varies; discuss complementary therapies with a clinician.

heading_notes.heading: Lifestyle and home remedies
notes: Gentle vulvar care, avoiding irritants, cotton underwear, cool packs, and lubricants may reduce discomfort.

heading_notes.heading: Coping and support
notes: Chronic pain support and open communication can help with sexual and emotional effects.

heading_notes.heading: Preparing for your appointment
notes: Bring symptom triggers, prior treatments, medicines, and questions about pain control.

heading_notes.heading: What you can do
notes: Track pain and exposures and ask about multidisciplinary care.

notes: Expect questions about pain location, triggers, sex/tampon use, infections, and prior treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Overview
notes: Vaginal yeast infection is overgrowth of Candida, causing irritation and inflammation; it is common and usually treatable.

heading_notes.heading: Products & Services
notes: Product or service listings are linked here; no disorder-specific clinical guidance.

heading_notes.heading: Symptoms
notes: Intense vaginal/vulvar itching, soreness, burning, redness, pain with sex/urination, and thick white discharge may occur.

heading_notes.heading: Complicated yeast infection
notes: Severe, recurrent, non-albicans, or infection in someone with diabetes/immunosuppression may require longer or different treatment.

heading_notes.heading: When to see a doctor
notes: Seek evaluation for first episode, recurrent symptoms, pregnancy, severe symptoms, or failure of over-the-counter treatment.

heading_notes.heading: Causes
notes: Candida normally may be present; antibiotics, hormonal changes, pregnancy, diabetes, or immune suppression can allow overgrowth.

heading_notes.heading: Risk factors
notes: Antibiotics, pregnancy/high estrogen, uncontrolled diabetes, immune suppression, and some contraceptive factors may increase risk.

heading_notes.heading: Prevention
notes: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics and scented vaginal products, keep the area dry, and manage diabetes; preventive medicines may be used for recurrent cases.

Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis may begin with pelvic examination; ultrasound can confirm and map fibroids, while blood tests assess causes of bleeding or anemia. Depending on the clinical question, further imaging or hysteroscopy may be used. Management is individualized and can include observation, symptom-targeting medicines, noninvasive or minimally invasive procedures, myomectomy, or hysterectomy; no single option is best for everyone.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) - Diagnosis & treatment - Mayo Clinic
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: No single test diagnoses PID. Assessment combines history, symptoms, pelvic examination, and samples for infection testing; blood or urine tests and ultrasound may help, with laparoscopy or endometrial biopsy considered when diagnosis remains unclear. Treatment usually starts promptly with antibiotics and may be adjusted to test results; partners may need treatment. Hospital care or rarely drainage/surgery may be needed for severe illness, abscess, pregnancy, or lack of response.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Cervicitis - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis includes physical and pelvic examination, cervical/vaginal fluid sampling for infection testing, and sometimes urine testing. Management depends on cause: stopping an irritating product may resolve a reaction; cervicitis caused by an STI commonly requires antibiotics for the patient and partners; antiviral medicine may be offered for herpes. Repeat testing may be recommended for some infections.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: NCBI Bookshelf (NIH): Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections, StatPearls — Chronic urinary tract infections
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Recurrent UTI is defined as at least two symptomatic acute cystitis episodes in six months or at least three in one year. Typical symptoms include painful urination, urgency, frequency, and suprapubic pain; fever, chills, flank pain, nausea, or vomiting suggest possible kidney involvement. Most recurrent infections are new infections rather than relapses; Escherichia coli causes most cases, and risks include frequent intercourse, spermicide-containing diaphragms, menopause, and untreated vaginal atrophy.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: NCBI Bookshelf (NIH): Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections, StatPearls — Chronic urinary tract infections
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis should be supported by documented positive urine cultures together with compatible urinary symptoms; culture and susceptibility testing help guide therapy. Routine cystoscopy or imaging is usually unnecessary, but imaging is considered for relapses, persistent hematuria, stone history, or repeated Proteus isolation. Treatment uses appropriately selected antibiotics; prevention options include hygiene measures, hydration, vaginal estrogen when appropriate, and selected preventive antibiotic strategies.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Interstitial cystitis is a chronic painful bladder condition; pain often increases as the bladder fills and improves temporarily after urination. Symptoms can include pelvic or lower-abdominal pressure or tenderness, urinary frequency, urgency, and pain during sex. The exact cause is uncertain; possible symptom flare triggers include irritating products, some foods or drinks, physical activity, and sexual activity.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH — Interstitial cystitis
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis is based on the symptom history, physical examination, and laboratory or other tests while ruling out conditions with similar symptoms, including infection. A bladder diary and urine testing may be used; cystoscopy or other testing can be used when clinically indicated. Management may combine diet or lifestyle changes, bladder training, pelvic-floor physical therapy, medicines, bladder instillation or stretching, neuromodulation, and occasionally surgery.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH — Urinary retention
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Acute retention can cause inability to urinate, severe lower-abdominal pain, urgent need to urinate, and lower-abdominal swelling. Chronic retention may have few or no symptoms, or may cause incomplete emptying, frequent small voids, hesitancy, weak stream, urgency with little output, post-void urge, leakage, or lower-abdominal discomfort. Retention results from a blockage of urine flow or inadequate bladder contraction.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH — Urinary retention
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Evaluation uses medical history, physical examination, postvoid residual measurement, urinalysis and other laboratory tests, imaging, urodynamics, and sometimes cystoscopy. Treatment depends on whether retention is acute or chronic and on its cause; options include catheter drainage, medicines, procedures or devices, surgery, and self-care. Acute retention requires prompt bladder drainage with a catheter to relieve pain and reduce risk of bladder or kidney damage.

headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: Pelvic floor support problems can allow the womb, bladder, or bowel to bulge into the vagina. Possible symptoms include pelvic or vaginal pressure, a vaginal bulge, constipation, and urinary frequency, incomplete emptying, or leakage. Risk factors include vaginal childbirth, increasing age, obesity, pelvic surgery, and chronic straining or increased abdominal pressure.

Symptoms & causes.summary: Vaginal prolapse results from weakness or laxity in the ligaments, fascia, and muscles supporting the pelvic organs, allowing an organ to protrude into the vagina. Symptoms can include vaginal pressure or fullness, a visible or palpable bulge, urinary difficulties or leakage, constipation, and discomfort during sex.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: ACOG — Ovarian Cysts — Dermoid cyst
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: An ovarian dermoid cyst (teratoma) is generally a benign mass containing mature tissue types such as skin and hair; it may be present from birth and enlarge during reproductive years. Many cause no symptoms, but pain may occur; a larger cyst can twist the ovary, while bleeding or rupture can cause sudden severe pain.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: ACOG — Ovarian Cysts — Dermoid cyst
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Ultrasound assesses the cyst's size, location, and solid or fluid components; blood tests such as CA-125 may be used when cancer is a concern. Options include surveillance with repeat ultrasound or surgery when the cyst is large, symptomatic, or suspicious; surgery may be cystectomy or removal of the ovary.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: NHS — Vaginismus
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: The vaginal muscles tighten involuntarily when penetration is attempted, which may produce burning or stinging pain. Triggers can include tampon insertion, penetrative sex, cervical screening or even an object approaching the vagina; other contributors to vaginal pain include thrush, STIs, menopause, pelvic inflammatory disease and endometriosis.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: Cleveland Clinic — Vaginal cysts
headings: Symptoms, causes and key clinical features
Symptoms & causes.summary: A vaginal cyst is a fluid-, mucus-, pus- or air-filled lump; it may be unnoticed, but can appear as a bump and become painful, swollen or discolored when infected. Common mechanisms include childbirth-related or other vaginal-wall injury and blockage of a gland or duct; examples include Bartholin, inclusion, Gartner-duct and Müllerian cysts.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) - Diagnosis & treatment - Mayo Clinic
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: PMS has no unique examination finding or laboratory test. A symptom diary across at least two menstrual cycles can establish a predictable pattern, and testing may assess lookalike conditions such as thyroid or mood disorders. Treatment is based on severity and may include lifestyle measures, medicines such as SSRIs or NSAIDs, diuretics, or hormonal contraception.

Diagnosis & treatment.page_title: Trichomoniasis - Diagnosis & treatment - Mayo Clinic
Diagnosis & treatment.summary: Diagnosis may use genital examination and a fluid sample examined under a microscope; molecular testing or culture may follow when needed, and testing for other STIs may be offered. Medication choice and pregnancy considerations require clinician review.

Symptoms & causes.page_title: USPSTF, Cervical Cancer: Screening — Cervical cancer screening
Symptoms & causes.summary: Screen people who have a cervix for cervical precancer and cancer according to age, prior results, anatomy, and risk; ensure abnormal results receive appropriate evaluation and treatment. USPSTF recommends cytology alone every 3 years for ages 21–29; for ages 30–65, cytology every 3 years, primary hrHPV testing every 5 years, or cotesting every 5 years.

diagnostic_profile_augmentation.methodology: Structured educational diagnostic-profile augmentation. Tests are marked primary, adjunct, conditional, or not routinely indicated; non-indication is not a negative result. Findings are generalized from established OB/GYN diagnostic practice and require clinician/local-guideline review before clinical use.
diagnostic_profile_augmentation.scope_limits: This is not a clinical decision support rule, order set, diagnostic threshold source, or patient-specific recommendation. Numeric reference ranges are intentionally omitted because they depend on assay, gestational age, laboratory, and guideline.

clinic_probability_model.population_and_denominator: One encounter in a general large-city U.S./global outpatient OBGYN clinic with a mixed preventive, gynecologic, contraception, prenatal, postpartum, and referred-problem caseload.
clinic_probability_model.measure: Probability that a condition or routine-care service is identified, actively managed, or materially screened at that encounter.
not_a_measure_of: risk of a condition in an asymptomatic person
clinic_probability_model.interpretation: Context values are modeled conditional relevance estimates. Contexts overlap, so values across contexts and records must not be summed.
clinic_probability_model.calibration: Values combine broad outpatient clinical prevalence patterns with visit-context relevance; they are not extracted as measured rates from a single dataset.
routine_care_model_notes: This is a synthesis of the cited guidance, not a substitute for local protocols, clinician judgment, or individualized care.
Guidelines differ by country and by risk group; U.S. screening intervals and NICE/WHO antenatal or postnatal service models should not be treated as interchangeable mandates.

Routine preventive visits should be individualized. A pelvic examination or clinical breast examination is not universally indicated for every asymptomatic patient; symptoms, history, risk, screening needs, patient preferences, and shared decision-making determine whether it is appropriate.

USPSTF cervical-screening recommendations cited here are dated 2018 and the page identifies an update in progress; verify the current recommendation and any ACOG/ASCCP end-stage management guidance before implementation.
